 tensor([0.1288], requires_grad=True)]

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: We can also get the state (what the model contains) of the model using .state_dict() .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: # List named parameters model_0 . state_dict ()

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: OrderedDict([('weights', tensor([0.3367])), ('bias', tensor([0.1288]))])

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: Notice how the values for weights and bias from model_0.state_dict() come out as random float tensors?

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: This is because we initialized them above using torch.randn() .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: Essentially we want to start from random parameters and get the model to update them towards parameters that fit our data best (the hardcoded weight and bias values we set when creating our straight line data).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: Exercise: Try changing the torch.manual_seed() value two cells above, see what happens to the weights and bias values.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Checking the contents of a PyTorch model
text: Because our model starts with random values, right now it'll have poor predictive power.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: To check this we can pass it the test data X_test to see how closely it predicts y_test .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: When we pass data to our model, it'll go through the model's forward() method and produce a result using the computation we've defined.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's make some predictions.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Make predictions with model with torch . inference_mode (): y_preds = model_0 ( X_test ) # Note: in older PyTorch code you might also see torch.no_grad() # with torch.no_grad(): #   y_preds = model_0(X_test)

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Hmm?

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: You probably noticed we used torch.inference_mode() as a context manager (that's what the with torch.inference_mode(): is) to make the predictions.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: As the name suggests, torch.inference_mode() is used when using a model for inference (making predictions).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: torch.inference_mode() turns off a bunch of things (like gradient tracking, which is necessary for training but not for inference) to make forward-passes (data going through the forward() method) faster.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Note: In older PyTorch code, you may also see torch.no_grad() being used for inference. While torch.inference_mode() and torch.no_grad() do similar things, torch.inference_mode() is newer, potentially faster and preferred. See this Tweet from PyTorch for more.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We've made some predictions, let's see what they look like.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Check the predictions print ( f "Number of testing samples: { len ( X_test ) } " ) print ( f "Number of predictions made: { len ( y_preds ) } " ) print ( f "Predicted values: \n { y_preds } " )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Notice how there's one prediction value per testing sample.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: This is because of the kind of data we're using. For our straight line, one X value maps to one y value.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: However, machine learning models are very flexible. You could have 100 X values mapping to one, two, three or 10 y values. It all depends on what you're working on.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Our predictions are still numbers on a page, let's visualize them with our plot_predictions() function we created above.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: plot_predictions ( predictions = y_preds )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: y_test - y_preds

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Woah! Those predictions look pretty bad...

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: This makes sense though, when you remember our model is just using random parameter values to make predictions.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: It hasn't even looked at the blue dots to try to predict the green dots.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Time to change that.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Right now our model is making predictions using random parameters to make calculations, it's basically guessing (randomly).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: To fix that, we can update its internal parameters (I also refer to parameters as patterns), the weights and bias values we set randomly using nn.Parameter() and torch.randn() to be something that better represents the data.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We could hard code this (since we know the default values weight=0.7 and bias=0.3 ) but where's the fun in that?

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Much of the time you won't know what the ideal parameters are for a model.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Instead, it's much more fun to write code to see if the model can try and figure them out itself.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: For our model to update its parameters on its own, we'll need to add a few more things to our recipe.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: And that's a loss function as well as an optimizer .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: The rolls of these are:

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: Let's create a loss function and an optimizer we can use to help improve our model.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: Depending on what kind of problem you're working on will depend on what loss function and what optimizer you use.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: However, there are some common values, that are known to work well such as the SGD (stochastic gradient descent) or Adam optimizer. And the MAE (mean absolute error) loss function for regression problems (predicting a number) or binary cross entropy loss function for classification problems (predicting one thing or another).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: For our problem, since we're predicting a number, let's use MAE (which is under torch.nn.L1Loss() ) in PyTorch as our loss function.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: Mean absolute error (MAE, in PyTorch: torch.nn.L1Loss ) measures the absolute difference between two points (predictions and labels) and then takes the mean across all examples.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: And we'll use SGD, torch.optim.SGD(params, lr) where:

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: params is the target model parameters you'd like to optimize (e.g. the weights and bias values we randomly set before).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: lr is the learning rate you'd like the optimizer to update the parameters at, higher means the optimizer will try larger updates (these can sometimes be too large and the optimizer will fail to work), lower means the optimizer will try smaller updates (these can sometimes be too small and the optimizer will take too long to find the ideal values). The learning rate is considered a hyperparameter (because it's set by a machine learning engineer). Common starting values for the learning rate are 0.01 , 0.001 , 0.0001 , however, these can also be adjusted over time (this is called learning rate scheduling ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: Woah, that's a lot, let's see it in code.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating a loss function and optimizer in PyTorch
text: # Create the loss function loss_fn = nn . L1Loss () # MAE loss is same as L1Loss # Create the optimizer optimizer = torch . optim . SGD ( params = model_0 . parameters (), # parameters of target model to optimize lr = 0.01 ) # learning rate (how much the optimizer should change parameters at each step, higher=more (less stable), lower=less (might take a long time))

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: Woohoo! Now we've got a loss function and an optimizer, it's now time to create a training loop (and testing loop ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: The training loop involves the model going through the training data and learning the relationships between the features and labels .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: The testing loop involves going through the testing data and evaluating how good the patterns are that the model learned on the training data (the model never sees the testing data during training).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: Each of these is called a "loop" because we want our model to look (loop through) at each sample in each dataset.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: To create these we're going to write a Python for loop in the theme of the unofficial PyTorch optimization loop song (there's a video version too ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: The unofficial PyTorch optimization loops song, a fun way to remember the steps in a PyTorch training (and testing) loop.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Creating an optimization loop in PyTorch
text: There will be a fair bit of code but nothing we can't handle.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: For the training loop, we'll build the following steps:

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Note: The above is just one example of how the steps could be ordered or described. With experience you'll find making PyTorch training loops can be quite flexible.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: And on the ordering of things, the above is a good default order but you may see slightly different orders. Some rules of thumb:

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Calculate the loss ( loss = ... ) before performing backpropagation on it ( loss.backward() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Zero gradients ( optimizer.zero_grad() ) before computing the gradients of the loss with respect to every model parameter ( loss.backward() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Step the optimizer ( optimizer.step() ) after performing backpropagation on the loss ( loss.backward() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: For resources to help understand what's happening behind the scenes with backpropagation and gradient descent, see the extra-curriculum section.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: As for the testing loop (evaluating our model), the typical steps include:

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Notice the testing loop doesn't contain performing backpropagation ( loss.backward() ) or stepping the optimizer ( optimizer.step() ), this is because no parameters in the model are being changed during testing, they've already been calculated. For testing, we're only interested in the output of the forward pass through the model.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's put all of the above together and train our model for 100 epochs (forward passes through the data) and we'll evaluate it every 10 epochs.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Set the number of epochs (how many times the model will pass over the training data) epochs = 100 # Create empty loss lists to track values train_loss_values = [] test_loss_values = [] epoch_count = [] for epoch in range ( epochs ): ### Training # Put model in training mode (this is the default state of a model) model_0 . train () # 1. Forward pass on train data using the forward() method inside y_pred = model_0 ( X_train ) # print(y_pred) # 2. Calculate the loss (how different are our models predictions to the ground truth) loss = loss_fn ( y_pred , y_train ) # 3. Zero grad of the optimizer optimizer . zero_grad () # 4. Loss backwards loss . backward () # 5. Progress the optimizer optimizer . step () ### Testing # Put the model in evaluation mode model_0 . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): # 1. Forward pass on test data test_pred = model_0 ( X_test ) # 2. Caculate loss on test data test_loss = loss_fn ( test_pred , y_test . type ( torch . float )) # predictions come in torch.float datatype, so comparisons need to be done with tensors of the same type # Print out what's happening if epoch % 10 == 0 : epoch_count . append ( epoch ) train_loss_values . append ( loss . detach () . numpy ()) test_loss_values . append ( test_loss . detach () . numpy ()) print ( f "Epoch: { epoch } | MAE Train Loss: { loss } | MAE Test Loss: { test_loss } " )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Oh would you look at that! Looks like our loss is going down with every epoch, let's plot it to find out.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Plot the loss curves plt . plot ( epoch_count , train_loss_values , label = "Train loss" ) plt . plot ( epoch_count , test_loss_values , label = "Test loss" ) plt . title ( "Training and test loss curves" ) plt . ylabel ( "Loss" ) plt . xlabel ( "Epochs" ) plt . legend ();

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Nice! The loss curves show the loss going down over time. Remember, loss is the measure of how wrong your model is, so the lower the better.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: But why did the loss go down?

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Well, thanks to our loss function and optimizer, the model's internal parameters ( weights and bias ) were updated to better reflect the underlying patterns in the data.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's inspect our model's .state_dict() to see how close our model gets to the original values we set for weights and bias.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Find our model's learned parameters print ( "The model learned the following values for weights and bias:" ) print ( model_0 . state_dict ()) print ( " \n And the original values for weights and bias are:" ) print ( f "weights: { weight } , bias: { bias } " )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
The model learned the following values for weights and bias:
OrderedDict([('weights', tensor([0.5784])), ('bias', tensor([0.3513]))])

And the original values for weights and bias are:
weights: 0.7, bias: 0.3

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Wow! How cool is that?

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Our model got very close to calculating the exact original values for weight and bias (and it would probably get even closer if we trained it for longer).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Exercise: Try changing the epochs value above to 200, what happens to the loss curves and the weights and bias parameter values of the model?

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: It'd likely never guess them perfectly (especially when using more complicated datasets) but that's okay, often you can do very cool things with a close approximation.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: This is the whole idea of machine learning and deep learning, there are some ideal values that describe our data and rather than figuring them out by hand, we can train a model to figure them out programmatically .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: Once you've trained a model, you'll likely want to make predictions with it.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: We've already seen a glimpse of this in the training and testing code above, the steps to do it outside of the training/testing loop are similar.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: There are three things to remember when making predictions (also called performing inference) with a PyTorch model:

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: Set the model in evaluation mode ( model.eval() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: Make the predictions using the inference mode context manager ( with torch.inference_mode(): ... ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: All predictions should be made with objects on the same device (e.g. data and model on GPU only or data and model on CPU only).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: The first two items make sure all helpful calculations and settings PyTorch uses behind the scenes during training but aren't necessary for inference are turned off (this results in faster computation). And the third ensures that you won't run into cross-device errors.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: # 1. Set the model in evaluation mode model_0 . eval () # 2. Setup the inference mode context manager with torch . inference_mode (): # 3. Make sure the calculations are done with the model and data on the same device # in our case, we haven't setup device-agnostic code yet so our data and model are # on the CPU by default. # model_0.to(device) # X_test = X_test.to(device) y_preds = model_0 ( X_test ) y_preds

section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)
text: Nice! We've made some predictions with our trained model, now how do they look?

section: 4. Making predictions with a trained PyTorch model (inference)

text: Let's get onto saving and reloading a model in PyTorch.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 5. Saving and loading a PyTorch model
text: If you've trained a PyTorch model, chances are you'll want to save it and export it somewhere.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 5. Saving and loading a PyTorch model
text: As in, you might train it on Google Colab or your local machine with a GPU but you'd like to now export it to some sort of application where others can use it.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 5. Saving and loading a PyTorch model
text: Or maybe you'd like to save your progress on a model and come back and load it back later.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 5. Saving and loading a PyTorch model
text: For saving and loading models in PyTorch, there are three main methods you should be aware of (all of below have been taken from the PyTorch saving and loading models guide ):

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: 5. Saving and loading a PyTorch model
text: Note: As stated in Python's pickle documentation , the pickle module is not secure . That means you should only ever unpickle (load) data you trust. That goes for loading PyTorch models as well. Only ever use saved PyTorch models from sources you trust.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: The recommended way for saving and loading a model for inference (making predictions) is by saving and loading a model's state_dict() .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's see how we can do that in a few steps:

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll create a directory for saving models to called models using Python's pathlib module.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll create a file path to save the model to.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll call torch.save(obj, f) where obj is the target model's state_dict() and f is the filename of where to save the model.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Note: It's common convention for PyTorch saved models or objects to end with .pt or .pth , like saved_model_01.pth .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: from pathlib import Path # 1. Create models directory MODEL_PATH = Path ( "models" ) MODEL_PATH . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) # 2. Create model save path MODEL_NAME = "01_pytorch_workflow_model_0.pth" MODEL_SAVE_PATH = MODEL_PATH / MODEL_NAME # 3. Save the model state dict print ( f "Saving model to: { MODEL_SAVE_PATH } " ) torch . save ( obj = model_0 . state_dict (), # only saving the state_dict() only saves the models learned parameters f = MODEL_SAVE_PATH )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Saving model to: models/01_pytorch_workflow_model_0.pth

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Check the saved file path ! ls - l models / 01 _pytorch_workflow_model_0 . pth

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: -rw-rw-r-- 1 daniel daniel 1063 Nov 10 16:07 models/01_pytorch_workflow_model_0.pth

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Since we've now got a saved model state_dict() at models/01_pytorch_workflow_model_0.pth we can now load it in using torch.nn.Module.load_state_dict(torch.load(f)) where f is the filepath of our saved model state_dict() .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Why call torch.load() inside torch.nn.Module.load_state_dict() ?

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Because we only saved the model's state_dict() which is a dictionary of learned parameters and not the entire model, we first have to load the state_dict() with torch.load() and then pass that state_dict() to a new instance of our model (which is a subclass of nn.Module ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Why not save the entire model?

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Saving the entire model rather than just the state_dict() is more intuitive, however, to quote the PyTorch documentation (italics mine):

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: The disadvantage of this approach (saving the whole model) is that the serialized data is bound to the specific classes and the exact directory structure used when the model is saved...

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Because of this, your code can break in various ways when used in other projects or after refactors.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: So instead, we're using the flexible method of saving and loading just the state_dict() , which again is basically a dictionary of model parameters.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Let's test it out by creating another instance of LinearRegressionModel() , which is a subclass of torch.nn.Module and will hence have the in-built method load_state_dict() .

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: # Instantiate a new instance of our model (this will be instantiated with random weights) loaded_model_0 = LinearRegressionModel () # Load the state_dict of our saved model (this will update the new instance of our model with trained weights) loaded_model_0 . load_state_dict ( torch . load ( f = MODEL_SAVE_PATH ))

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: <All keys matched successfully>

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Excellent! It looks like things matched up.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Now to test our loaded model, let's perform inference with it (make predictions) on the test data.

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Remember the rules for performing inference with PyTorch models?

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: If not, here's a refresher:

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Set the model in evaluation mode ( model.eval() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: Make the predictions using the inference mode context manager ( with torch.inference_mode(): ... ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: All predictions should be made with objects on the same device (e.g. data and model on GPU only or data and model on CPU only).

title: PytorchWorkflow
section: Loading a saved PyTorch model's state_dict()
text: # 1. Put the loaded model into evaluation mode loaded_model_0 . eval () # 2. Use the inference mode context manager to make predictions with torch . inference_mode (): loaded_model_preds = loaded_model_0 ( X_test ) # perform a forward pass on the test data with the loaded model

text: We've covered a fair bit of ground so far.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: But once you've had some practice, you'll be performing the above steps like dancing down the street.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Speaking of practice, let's put everything we've done so far together.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Except this time we'll make our code device agnostic (so if there's a GPU available, it'll use it and if not, it will default to the CPU).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: There'll be far less commentary in this section than above since what we're going to go through has already been covered.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll start by importing the standard libraries we need.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Note: If you're using Google Colab, to setup a GPU, go to Runtime -> Change runtime type -> Hardware acceleration -> GPU. If you do this, it will reset the Colab runtime and you will lose saved variables.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Import PyTorch and matplotlib import torch from torch import nn # nn contains all of PyTorch's building blocks for neural networks import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # Check PyTorch version torch . __version__

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Now let's start making our code device agnostic by setting device="cuda" if it's available, otherwise it'll default to device="cpu" .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Setup device agnostic code device = "cuda" if torch . cuda . is_available () else "cpu" print ( f "Using device: { device } " )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Using device: cuda

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: If you've got access to a GPU, the above should've printed out:

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Using device: cuda

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Otherwise, you'll be using a CPU for the following computations. This is fine for our small dataset but it will take longer for larger datasets.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's create some data just like before.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: First, we'll hard-code some weight and bias values.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Then we'll make a range of numbers between 0 and 1, these will be our X values.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Finally, we'll use the X values, as well as the weight and bias values to create y using the linear regression formula ( y = weight * X + bias ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Create weight and bias weight = 0.7 bias = 0.3 # Create range values start = 0 end = 1 step = 0.02 # Create X and y (features and labels) X = torch . arange ( start , end , step ) . unsqueeze ( dim = 1 ) # without unsqueeze, errors will happen later on (shapes within linear layers) y = weight * X + bias X [: 10 ], y [: 10 ]

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Wonderful!

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Now we've got some data, let's split it into training and test sets.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll use an 80/20 split with 80% training data and 20% testing data.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Split data train_split = int ( 0.8 * len ( X )) X_train , y_train = X [: train_split ], y [: train_split ] X_test , y_test = X [ train_split :], y [ train_split :] len ( X_train ), len ( y_train ), len ( X_test ), len ( y_test )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Excellent, let's visualize them to make sure they look okay.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Note: If you've reset your runtime, this function won't work, # you'll have to rerun the cell above where it's instantiated. plot_predictions ( X_train , y_train , X_test , y_test )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We've got some data, now it's time to make a model.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll create the same style of model as before except this time, instead of defining the weight and bias parameters of our model manually using nn.Parameter() , we'll use nn.Linear(in_features, out_features) to do it for us.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Where in_features is the number of dimensions your input data has and out_features is the number of dimensions you'd like it to be output to.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: In our case, both of these are 1 since our data has 1 input feature ( X ) per label ( y ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Creating a linear regression model using nn.Parameter versus using nn.Linear . There are plenty more examples of where the torch.nn module has pre-built computations, including many popular and useful neural network layers.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Subclass nn.Module to make our model class LinearRegressionModelV2 ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self ): super () . __init__ () # Use nn.Linear() for creating the model parameters self . linear_layer = nn . Linear ( in_features = 1 , out_features = 1 ) # Define the forward computation (input data x flows through nn.Linear()) def forward ( self , x : torch . Tensor ) -> torch . Tensor : return self . linear_layer ( x ) # Set the manual seed when creating the model (this isn't always needed but is used for demonstrative purposes, try commenting it out and seeing what happens) torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) model_1 = LinearRegressionModelV2 () model_1 , model_1 . state_dict ()

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
(LinearRegressionModelV2(
   (linear_layer): Linear(in_features=1, out_features=1, bias=True)
 ),
 OrderedDict([('linear_layer.weight', tensor([[0.7645]])),
              ('linear_layer.bias', tensor([0.8300]))]))

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Notice the outputs of model_1.state_dict() , the nn.Linear() layer created a random weight and bias parameter for us.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Now let's put our model on the GPU (if it's available).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We can change the device our PyTorch objects are on using .to(device) .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: First let's check the model's current device.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Check model device next ( model_1 . parameters ()) . device

title: PytorchWorkflow

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Wonderful, looks like the model's on the CPU by default.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's change it to be on the GPU (if it's available).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Set model to GPU if it's available, otherwise it'll default to CPU model_1 . to ( device ) # the device variable was set above to be "cuda" if available or "cpu" if not next ( model_1 . parameters ()) . device

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: device(type='cuda', index=0)

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Nice! Because of our device agnostic code, the above cell will work regardless of whether a GPU is available or not.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: If you do have access to a CUDA-enabled GPU, you should see an output of something like:

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: device(type='cuda', index=0)

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Time to build a training and testing loop.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: First we'll need a loss function and an optimizer.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's use the same functions we used earlier, nn.L1Loss() and torch.optim.SGD() .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We'll have to pass the new model's parameters ( model.parameters() ) to the optimizer for it to adjust them during training.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: The learning rate of 0.01 worked well before too so let's use that again.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: # Create loss function loss_fn = nn . L1Loss () # Create optimizer optimizer = torch . optim . SGD ( params = model_1 . parameters (), # optimize newly created model's parameters lr = 0.01 )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Beautiful, loss function and optimizer ready, now let's train and evaluate our model using a training and testing loop.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: The only different thing we'll be doing in this step compared to the previous training loop is putting the data on the target device .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: We've already put our model on the target device using model_1.to(device) .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: And we can do the same with the data.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: That way if the model is on the GPU, the data is on the GPU (and vice versa).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Let's step things up a notch this time and set epochs=1000 .

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: If you need a reminder of the PyTorch training loop steps, see below.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
Forward pass - The model goes through all of the training data once, performing its forward() function
            calculations ( model(x_train) ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
Calculate the loss - The model's outputs (predictions) are compared to the ground truth and evaluated
            to see how
            wrong they are ( loss = loss_fn(y_pred, y_train ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
Zero gradients - The optimizers gradients are set to zero (they are accumulated by default) so they
            can be
            recalculated for the specific training step ( optimizer.zero_grad() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
Perform backpropagation on the loss - Computes the gradient of the loss with respect for every model
            parameter to
            be updated (each parameter
            with requires_grad=True ). This is known as backpropagation , hence "backwards"
            ( loss.backward() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text:
Step the optimizer (gradient descent) - Update the parameters with requires_grad=True with respect to the loss
            gradients in order to improve them ( optimizer.step() ).

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Set the number of epochs epochs = 1000 # Put data on the available device # Without this, error will happen (not all model/data on device) X_train = X_train . to ( device ) X_test = X_test . to ( device ) y_train = y_train . to ( device ) y_test = y_test . to ( device ) for epoch in range ( epochs ): ### Training model_1 . train () # train mode is on by default after construction # 1. Forward pass y_pred = model_1 ( X_train ) # 2. Calculate loss loss = loss_fn ( y_pred , y_train ) # 3. Zero grad optimizer optimizer . zero_grad () # 4. Loss backward loss . backward () # 5. Step the optimizer optimizer . step () ### Testing model_1 . eval () # put the model in evaluation mode for testing (inference) # 1. Forward pass with torch . inference_mode (): test_pred = model_1 ( X_test ) # 2. Calculate the loss test_loss = loss_fn ( test_pred , y_test ) if epoch % 100 == 0 : print ( f "Epoch: { epoch } | Train loss: { loss } | Test loss: { test_loss } " )

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Note: Due to the random nature of machine learning, you will likely get slightly different results (different loss and prediction values) depending on whether your model was trained on CPU or GPU. This is true even if you use the same random seed on either device. If the difference is large, you may want to look for errors, however, if it is small (ideally it is), you can ignore it.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Nice! That loss looks pretty low.

title: PytorchWorkflow

title: PytorchWorkflow

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Ho ho! Now that's pretty darn close to a perfect model.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Remember though, in practice, it's rare that you'll know the perfect parameters ahead of time.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: And if you knew the parameters your model had to learn ahead of time, what would be the fun of machine learning?

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: Plus, in many real-world machine learning problems, the number of parameters can well exceed tens of millions.

title: PytorchWorkflow
text: I don't know about you but I'd rather write code for a computer to figure those out rather than doing it by hand.

title: PytorchWorkflow

That means the data is on CUDA device 0 (the first GPU your system has access to due to zero-indexing), if you end up using multiple GPUs in the future, this number may be higher.

text: Note: Many data science libraries such as pandas, matplotlib and NumPy aren't capable of using data that is stored on GPU. To fix this, you can call .cpu() on your target tensor to return a copy of your target tensor on the CPU.

Create model save path MODEL_NAME = "01_pytorch_workflow_model_1.pth" MODEL_SAVE_PATH = MODEL_PATH / MODEL_NAME # 3. Save the model state dict print ( f "Saving model to: { MODEL_SAVE_PATH } " ) torch . save ( obj = model_1 . state_dict (), # only saving the state_dict() only saves the models learned parameters f = MODEL_SAVE_PATH )

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: We've got some data ready, now it's time to build a model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: We'll break it down into a few parts.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Setting up device agnostic code (so our model can run on CPU or GPU if it's available).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Constructing a model by subclassing nn.Module .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Defining a loss function and optimizer.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Creating a training loop (this'll be in the next section).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The good news is we've been through all of the above steps before in notebook 01.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Except now we'll be adjusting them so they work with a classification dataset.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Let's start by importing PyTorch and torch.nn as well as setting up device agnostic code.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Standard PyTorch imports import torch from torch import nn # Make device agnostic code device = "cuda" if torch . cuda . is_available () else "cpu" device

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: 'cuda'

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Excellent, now device is setup, we can use it for any data or models we create and PyTorch will handle it on the CPU (default) or GPU if it's available.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: How about we create a model?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: We'll want a model capable of handling our X data as inputs and producing something in the shape of our y data as outputs.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: In other words, given X (features) we want our model to predict y (label).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: This setup where you have features and labels is referred to as supervised learning . Because your data is telling your model what the outputs should be given a certain input.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: To create such a model it'll need to handle the input and output shapes of X and y .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Remember how I said input and output shapes are important? Here we'll see why.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Let's create a model class that:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Subclasses nn.Module (almost all PyTorch models are subclasses of nn.Module ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Creates 2 nn.Linear layers in the constructor capable of handling the input and output shapes of X and y .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Defines a forward() method containing the forward pass computation of the model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Instantiates the model class and sends it to the target device .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # 1. Construct a model class that subclasses nn.Module class CircleModelV0 ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self ): super () . __init__ () # 2. Create 2 nn.Linear layers capable of handling X and y input and output shapes self . layer_1 = nn . Linear ( in_features = 2 , out_features = 5 ) # takes in 2 features (X), produces 5 features self . layer_2 = nn . Linear ( in_features = 5 , out_features = 1 ) # takes in 5 features, produces 1 feature (y) # 3. Define a forward method containing the forward pass computation def forward ( self , x ): # Return the output of layer_2, a single feature, the same shape as y return self . layer_2 ( self . layer_1 ( x )) # computation goes through layer_1 first then the output of layer_1 goes through layer_2 # 4. Create an instance of the model and send it to target device model_0 = CircleModelV0 () . to ( device ) model_0

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
CircleModelV0(
  (layer_1): Linear(in_features=2, out_features=5, bias=True)
  (layer_2): Linear(in_features=5, out_features=1, bias=True)
)

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: What's going on here?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: We've seen a few of these steps before.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The only major change is what's happening between self.layer_1 and self.layer_2 .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: self.layer_1 takes 2 input features in_features=2 and produces 5 output features out_features=5 .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: This is known as having 5 hidden units or neurons .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: This layer turns the input data from having 2 features to 5 features.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Why do this?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: This allows the model to learn patterns from 5 numbers rather than just 2 numbers, potentially leading to better outputs.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: I say potentially because sometimes it doesn't work.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The number of hidden units you can use in neural network layers is a hyperparameter (a value you can set yourself) and there's no set in stone value you have to use.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Generally more is better but there's also such a thing as too much. The amount you choose will depend on your model type and dataset you're working with.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Since our dataset is small and simple, we'll keep it small.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The only rule with hidden units is that the next layer, in our case, self.layer_2 has to take the same in_features as the previous layer out_features .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: That's why self.layer_2 has in_features=5 , it takes the out_features=5 from self.layer_1 and performs a linear computation on them, turning them into out_features=1 (the same shape as y ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: A visual example of what a similar classification neural network to the one we've just built looks like. Try creating one of your own on the TensorFlow Playground website .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: You can also do the same as above using nn.Sequential .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: nn.Sequential performs a forward pass computation of the input data through the layers in the order they appear.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Replicate CircleModelV0 with nn.Sequential model_0 = nn . Sequential ( nn . Linear ( in_features = 2 , out_features = 5 ), nn . Linear ( in_features = 5 , out_features = 1 ) ) . to ( device ) model_0

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=2, out_features=5, bias=True)
  (1): Linear(in_features=5, out_features=1, bias=True)
)

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Woah, that looks much simpler than subclassing nn.Module , why not just always use nn.Sequential ?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: nn.Sequential is fantastic for straight-forward computations, however, as the namespace says, it always runs in sequential order.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: So if you'd like something else to happen (rather than just straight-forward sequential computation) you'll want to define your own custom nn.Module subclass.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: We've setup a loss (also called a criterion or cost function) and optimizer before in notebook 01 .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: But different problem types require different loss functions.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: For example, for a regression problem (predicting a number) you might use mean absolute error (MAE) loss.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: And for a binary classification problem (like ours), you'll often use binary cross entropy as the loss function.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: However, the same optimizer function can often be used across different problem spaces.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: For example, the stochastic gradient descent optimizer (SGD, torch.optim.SGD() ) can be used for a range of problems, and the same applies to the Adam optimizer ( torch.optim.Adam() ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Table of various loss functions and optimizers, there are more but these are some common ones you'll see.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Since we're working with a binary classification problem, let's use a binary cross entropy loss function.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Note: Recall a loss function is what measures how wrong your model predictions are, the higher the loss, the worse your model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Also, PyTorch documentation often refers to loss functions as "loss criterion" or "criterion", these are all different ways of describing the same thing.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: PyTorch has two binary cross entropy implementations:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: torch.nn.BCELoss() - Creates a loss function that measures the binary cross entropy between the target (label) and input (features).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() - This is the same as above except it has a sigmoid layer ( nn.Sigmoid ) built-in (we'll see what this means soon).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Which one should you use?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The documentation for torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss() states that it's more numerically stable than using torch.nn.BCELoss() after a nn.Sigmoid layer.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: So generally, implementation 2 is a better option. However for advanced usage, you may want to separate the combination of nn.Sigmoid and torch.nn.BCELoss() but that is beyond the scope of this notebook.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Knowing this, let's create a loss function and an optimizer.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: For the optimizer we'll use torch.optim.SGD() to optimize the model parameters with learning rate 0.1.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Note: There's a discussion on the PyTorch forums about the use of nn.BCELoss vs. nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss . It can be confusing at first but as with many things, it becomes easier with practice.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Create a loss function # loss_fn = nn.BCELoss() # BCELoss = no sigmoid built-in loss_fn = nn . BCEWithLogitsLoss () # BCEWithLogitsLoss = sigmoid built-in # Create an optimizer optimizer = torch . optim . SGD ( params = model_0 . parameters (), lr = 0.1 )

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Now let's also create an evaluation metric .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: An evaluation metric can be used to offer another perspective on how your model is going.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: If a loss function measures how wrong your model is, I like to think of evaluation metrics as measuring how right it is.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Of course, you could argue both of these are doing the same thing but evaluation metrics offer a different perspective.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: After all, when evaluating your models it's good to look at things from multiple points of view.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: There are several evaluation metrics that can be used for classification problems but let's start out with accuracy .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Accuracy can be measured by dividing the total number of correct predictions over the total number of predictions.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: For example, a model that makes 99 correct predictions out of 100 will have an accuracy of 99%.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Let's write a function to do so.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Calculate accuracy (a classification metric) def accuracy_fn ( y_true , y_pred ): correct = torch . eq ( y_true , y_pred ) . sum () . item () # torch.eq() calculates where two tensors are equal acc = ( correct / len ( y_pred )) * 100 return acc

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Excellent! We can now use this function whilst training our model to measure it's performance alongside the loss.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Okay, now we've got a loss function and optimizer ready to go, let's train a model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Do you remember the steps in a PyTorch training loop?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: If not, here's a reminder.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Steps in training:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
Forward pass - The model goes through all of the training data once, performing its forward() function
            calculations ( model(x_train) ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
Calculate the loss - The model's outputs (predictions) are compared to the ground truth and evaluated
            to see how
            wrong they are ( loss = loss_fn(y_pred, y_train ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
Zero gradients - The optimizers gradients are set to zero (they are accumulated by default) so they
            can be
            recalculated for the specific training step ( optimizer.zero_grad() ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
Perform backpropagation on the loss - Computes the gradient of the loss with respect for every model
            parameter to
            be updated (each parameter
            with requires_grad=True ). This is known as backpropagation , hence "backwards"
            ( loss.backward() ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text:
Step the optimizer (gradient descent) - Update the parameters with requires_grad=True with respect to the loss
            gradients in order to improve them ( optimizer.step() ).

text: Alright, we've discussed how to take our raw model outputs and convert them to prediction labels, now let's build a training loop.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 3.2 Building a training and testing loop
text: Let's start by training for 100 epochs and outputing the model's progress every 10 epochs.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 3.2 Building a training and testing loop
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Set the number of epochs epochs = 100 # Put data to target device X_train , y_train = X_train . to ( device ), y_train . to ( device ) X_test , y_test = X_test . to ( device ), y_test . to ( device ) # Build training and evaluation loop for epoch in range ( epochs ): ### Training model_0 . train () # 1. Forward pass (model outputs raw logits) y_logits = model_0 ( X_train ) . squeeze () # squeeze to remove extra `1` dimensions, this won't work unless model and data are on same device y_pred = torch . round ( torch . sigmoid ( y_logits )) # turn logits -> pred probs -> pred labls # 2. Calculate loss/accuracy # loss = loss_fn(torch.sigmoid(y_logits), # Using nn.BCELoss you need torch.sigmoid() #                y_train) loss = loss_fn ( y_logits , # Using nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss works with raw logits y_train ) acc = accuracy_fn ( y_true = y_train , y_pred = y_pred ) # 3. Optimizer zero grad optimizer . zero_grad () # 4. Loss backwards loss . backward () # 5. Optimizer step optimizer . step () ### Testing model_0 . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): # 1. Forward pass test_logits = model_0 ( X_test ) . squeeze () test_pred = torch . round ( torch . sigmoid ( test_logits )) # 2. Caculate loss/accuracy test_loss = loss_fn ( test_logits , y_test ) test_acc = accuracy_fn ( y_true = y_test , y_pred = test_pred ) # Print out what's happening every 10 epochs if epoch % 10 == 0 : print ( f "Epoch: { epoch } | Loss: { loss : .5f } , Accuracy: { acc : .2f } % | Test loss: { test_loss : .5f } , Test acc: { test_acc : .2f } %" )

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Build model with non-linear activation function from torch import nn class CircleModelV2 ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self ): super () . __init__ () self . layer_1 = nn . Linear ( in_features = 2 , out_features = 10 ) self . layer_2 = nn . Linear ( in_features = 10 , out_features = 10 ) self . layer_3 = nn . Linear ( in_features = 10 , out_features = 1 ) self . relu = nn . ReLU () # <- add in ReLU activation function # Can also put sigmoid in the model # This would mean you don't need to use it on the predictions # self.sigmoid = nn.Sigmoid() def forward ( self , x ): # Intersperse the ReLU activation function between layers return self . layer_3 ( self . relu ( self . layer_2 ( self . relu ( self . layer_1 ( x ))))) model_3 = CircleModelV2 () . to ( device ) print ( model_3 )

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: A rule of thumb is to put them in between hidden layers and just after the output layer, however, there is no set in stone option. text: Now let's see how the ReLU activation function influences it.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: And instead of using PyTorch's ReLU ( torch.nn.ReLU ), we'll recreate it ourselves.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The ReLU function turns all negatives to 0 and leaves the positive values as they are.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Create ReLU function by hand def relu ( x ): return torch . maximum ( torch . tensor ( 0 ), x ) # inputs must be tensors # Pass toy tensor through ReLU function relu ( A )

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: It looks like our ReLU function worked, all of the negative values are zeros.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Let's plot them.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Plot ReLU activated toy tensor plt . plot ( relu ( A ));

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Nice! That looks exactly like the shape of the ReLU function on the Wikipedia page for ReLU ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: How about we try the sigmoid function we've been using?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: The sigmoid function formula goes like so:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: $$ out_i = \frac{1}{1+e^{-input_i}} $$

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Or using $x$ as input:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Where $S$ stands for sigmoid, $e$ stands for exponential ( torch.exp() ) and $i$ stands for a particular element in a tensor.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Let's build a function to replicate the sigmoid function with PyTorch.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Create a custom sigmoid function def sigmoid ( x ): return 1 / ( 1 + torch . exp ( - x )) # Test custom sigmoid on toy tensor sigmoid ( A )

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Woah, those values look a lot like prediction probabilities we've seen earlier, let's see what they look like visualized.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Plot sigmoid activated toy tensor plt . plot ( sigmoid ( A ));

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Looking good! We've gone from a straight line to a curved line.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Now there's plenty more non-linear activation functions that exist in PyTorch that we haven't tried.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: But these two are two of the most common.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: And the point remains, what patterns could you draw using an unlimited amount of linear (straight) and non-linear (not straight) lines?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Almost anything right?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: That's exactly what our model is doing when we combine linear and non-linear functions.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Instead of telling our model what to do, we give it tools to figure out how to best discover patterns in the data.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: And those tools are linear and non-linear functions.

section: 8. Putting things together by building a multi-class PyTorch model
text: We've covered a fair bit.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8. Putting things together by building a multi-class PyTorch model
text: But now let's put it all together using a multi-class classification problem.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8. Putting things together by building a multi-class PyTorch model
text: Recall a binary classification problem deals with classifying something as one of two options (e.g. a photo as a cat photo or a dog photo) where as a multi-class classification problem deals with classifying something from a list of more than two options (e.g. classifying a photo as a cat a dog or a chicken).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8. Putting things together by building a multi-class PyTorch model
text: Example of binary vs. multi-class classification. Binary deals with two classes (one thing or another), where as multi-class classification can deal with any number of classes over two, for example, the popular ImageNet-1k dataset is used as a computer vision benchmark and has 1000 classes.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: To begin a multi-class classification problem, let's create some multi-class data.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: To do so, we can leverage Scikit-Learn's make_blobs() method.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: This method will create however many classes (using the centers parameter) we want.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Specifically, let's do the following:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Create some multi-class data with make_blobs() .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Turn the data into tensors (the default of make_blobs() is to use NumPy arrays).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Split the data into training and test sets using train_test_split() .

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Visualize the data.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: # Import dependencies import torch import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split # Set the hyperparameters for data creation NUM_CLASSES = 4 NUM_FEATURES = 2 RANDOM_SEED = 42 # 1. Create multi-class data X_blob , y_blob = make_blobs ( n_samples = 1000 , n_features = NUM_FEATURES , # X features centers = NUM_CLASSES , # y labels cluster_std = 1.5 , # give the clusters a little shake up (try changing this to 1.0, the default) random_state = RANDOM_SEED ) # 2. Turn data into tensors X_blob = torch . from_numpy ( X_blob ) . type ( torch . float ) y_blob = torch . from_numpy ( y_blob ) . type ( torch . LongTensor ) print ( X_blob [: 5 ], y_blob [: 5 ]) # 3. Split into train and test sets X_blob_train , X_blob_test , y_blob_train , y_blob_test = train_test_split ( X_blob , y_blob , test_size = 0.2 , random_state = RANDOM_SEED ) # 4. Plot data plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 7 )) plt . scatter ( X_blob [:, 0 ], X_blob [:, 1 ], c = y_blob , cmap = plt . cm . RdYlBu );

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
text: Nice! Looks like we've got some multi-class data ready to go.

text: We've created a few models in PyTorch so far.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: You might also be starting to get an idea of how flexible neural networks are.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: How about we build one similar to model_3 but this is still capable of handling multi-class data?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: To do so, let's create a subclass of nn.Module that takes in three hyperparameters:

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: input_features - the number of X features coming into the model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: output_features - the ideal numbers of output features we'd like (this will be equivalent to NUM_CLASSES or the number of classes in your multi-class classification problem).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: hidden_units - the number of hidden neurons we'd like each hidden layer to use.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: Since we're putting things together, let's setup some device agnostic code (we don't have to do this again in the same notebook, it's only a reminder).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: Then we'll create the model class using the hyperparameters above.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: # Create device agnostic code device = "cuda" if torch . cuda . is_available () else "cpu" device

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: 'cuda'

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.2 Building a multi-class classification model in PyTorch
text: from torch import nn # Build model class BlobModel ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self , input_features , output_features , hidden_units = 8 ): """Initializes all required hyperparameters for a multi-class classification model. Args: input_features (int): Number of input features to the model. out_features (int): Number of output features of the model (how many classes there are). hidden_units (int): Number of hidden units between layers, default 8. """ super () . __init__ () self . linear_layer_stack = nn . Sequential ( nn . Linear ( in_features = input_features , out_features = hidden_units ), # nn.ReLU(), # <- does our dataset require non-linear layers? (try uncommenting and see if the results change) nn . Linear ( in_features = hidden_units , out_features = hidden_units ), # nn.ReLU(), # <- does our dataset require non-linear layers? (try uncommenting and see if the results change) nn . Linear ( in_features = hidden_units , out_features = output_features ), # how many classes are there? ) def forward ( self , x ): return self . linear_layer_stack ( x ) # Create an instance of BlobModel and send it to the target device model_4 = BlobModel ( input_features = NUM_FEATURES , output_features = NUM_CLASSES , hidden_units = 8 ) . to ( device ) model_4

  )
)

text: Excellent! Our multi-class model is ready to go, let's create a loss function and optimizer for it.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.3 Creating a loss function and optimizer for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: Since we're working on a multi-class classification problem, we'll use the nn.CrossEntropyLoss() method as our loss function.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.3 Creating a loss function and optimizer for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: And we'll stick with using SGD with a learning rate of 0.1 for optimizing our model_4 parameters.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: So right now our model is outputing logits but what if we wanted to figure out exactly which label is was giving the sample?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: As in, how do we go from logits -> prediction probabilities -> prediction labels just like we did with the binary classification problem?

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: That's where the softmax activation function comes into play.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: The softmax function calculates the probability of each prediction class being the actual predicted class compared to all other possible classes.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: If this doesn't make sense, let's see in code.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: # Make prediction logits with model y_logits = model_4 ( X_blob_test . to ( device )) # Perform softmax calculation on logits across dimension 1 to get prediction probabilities y_pred_probs = torch . softmax ( y_logits , dim = 1 ) print ( y_logits [: 5 ]) print ( y_pred_probs [: 5 ])

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: Of course, right now this is just random guessing so it's got a 25% chance of being right (since there's four classes). But we can improve those chances by training the model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.4 Getting prediction probabilities for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: For a multi-class classification problem, to turn the logits into prediction probabilities , you use the softmax activation function ( torch.softmax ).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification

text: The index of the value with the highest prediction probability is the class number the model thinks is most likely given the input features for that sample (although this is a prediction, it doesn't mean it will be correct).

section: 8.5 Creating a training and testing loop for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: Alright, now we've got all of the preparation steps out of the way, let's write a training and testing loop to improve and evaluate our model.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.5 Creating a training and testing loop for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: We've done many of these steps before so much of this will be practice.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.5 Creating a training and testing loop for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: The only difference is that we'll be adjusting the steps to turn the model outputs (logits) to prediction probabilities (using the softmax activation function) and then to prediction labels (by taking the argmax of the output of the softmax activation function).

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.5 Creating a training and testing loop for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: Let's train the model for epochs=100 and evaluate it every 10 epochs.

title: NeuralNetworkClassification
section: 8.5 Creating a training and testing loop for a multi-class PyTorch model
text: # Fit the model torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Set number of epochs epochs = 100 # Put data to target device X_blob_train , y_blob_train = X_blob_train . to ( device ), y_blob_train . to ( device ) X_blob_test , y_blob_test = X_blob_test . to ( device ), y_blob_test . to ( device ) for epoch in range ( epochs ): ### Training model_4 . train () # 1. Forward pass y_logits = model_4 ( X_blob_train ) # model outputs raw logits y_pred = torch . softmax ( y_logits , dim = 1 ) . argmax ( dim = 1 ) # go from logits -> prediction probabilities -> prediction labels # print(y_logits) # 2. Calculate loss and accuracy loss = loss_fn ( y_logits , y_blob_train ) acc = accuracy_fn ( y_true = y_blob_train , y_pred = y_pred ) # 3. Optimizer zero grad optimizer . zero_grad () # 4. Loss backwards loss . backward () # 5. Optimizer step optimizer . step () ### Testing model_4 . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): # 1. Forward pass test_logits = model_4 ( X_blob_test ) test_pred = torch . softmax ( test_logits , dim = 1 ) . argmax ( dim = 1 ) # 2. Calculate test loss and accuracy test_loss = loss_fn ( test_logits , y_blob_test ) test_acc = accuracy_fn ( y_true = y_blob_test , y_pred = test_pred ) # Print out what's happening if epoch % 10 == 0 : print ( f "Epoch: { epoch } | Loss: { loss : .5f } , Acc: { acc : .2f } % | Test Loss: { test_loss : .5f } , Test Acc: { test_acc : .2f } %" )

title: PytorchVision

title: PytorchVision
text: To begin working on a computer vision problem, let's get a computer vision dataset.

title: PytorchVision
text: We're going to start with FashionMNIST.

title: PytorchVision
text: MNIST stands for Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology.

title: PytorchVision
text: The original MNIST dataset contains thousands of examples of handwritten digits (from 0 to 9) and was used to build computer vision models to identify numbers for postal services.

title: PytorchVision
text: FashionMNIST , made by Zalando Research, is a similar setup.

title: PytorchVision
text: Except it contains grayscale images of 10 different kinds of clothing.

title: PytorchVision
text: torchvision.datasets contains a lot of example datasets you can use to practice writing computer vision code on. FashionMNIST is one of those datasets. And since it has 10 different image classes (different types of clothing), it's a multi-class classification problem.

title: PytorchVision
text: Later, we'll be building a computer vision neural network to identify the different styles of clothing in these images.

title: PytorchVision
text: PyTorch has a bunch of common computer vision datasets stored in torchvision.datasets .

title: PytorchVision
text: Including FashionMNIST in torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST() .

title: PytorchVision
text: To download it, we provide the following parameters:

title: PytorchVision
text: root: str - which folder do you want to download the data to?

title: PytorchVision
text: train: Bool - do you want the training or test split?

title: PytorchVision
text: download: Bool - should the data be downloaded?

title: PytorchVision
text: transform: torchvision.transforms - what transformations would you like to do on the data?

title: PytorchVision
text: target_transform - you can transform the targets (labels) if you like too.

title: PytorchVision
text: Many other datasets in torchvision have these parameter options.

title: PytorchVision
text: # Setup training data train_data = datasets . FashionMNIST ( root = "data" , # where to download data to? train = True , # get training data download = True , # download data if it doesn't exist on disk transform = ToTensor (), # images come as PIL format, we want to turn into Torch tensors target_transform = None # you can transform labels as well ) # Setup testing data test_data = datasets . FashionMNIST ( root = "data" , train = False , # get test data download = True , transform = ToTensor () )

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: The shape of the image tensor is [1, 28, 28] or more specifically:

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: [color_channels=1, height=28, width=28]

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: Having color_channels=1 means the image is grayscale.

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: Various problems will have various input and output shapes. But the premise remains: encode data into numbers, build a model to find patterns in those numbers, convert those patterns into something meaningful.

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: If color_channels=3 , the image comes in pixel values for red, green and blue (this is also known as the RGB color model ).

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: The order of our current tensor is often referred to as CHW (Color Channels, Height, Width).

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: There's debate on whether images should be represented as CHW (color channels first) or HWC (color channels last).

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: Note: You'll also see NCHW and NHWC formats where N stands for number of images . For example if you have a batch_size=32 , your tensor shape may be [32, 1, 28, 28] . We'll cover batch sizes later.

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: PyTorch generally accepts NCHW (channels first) as the default for many operators.

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: However, PyTorch also explains that NHWC (channels last) performs better and is considered best practice .

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: For now, since our dataset and models are relatively small, this won't make too much of a difference.

title: PytorchVision
section: 1.1 Input and output shapes of a computer vision model
text: But keep it in mind for when you're working on larger image datasets and using convolutional neural networks (we'll see these later).

text: Hmmm, this dataset doesn't look too aesthetic.

title: PytorchVision
text: But the principles we're going to learn on how to build a model for it will be similar across a wide range of computer vision problems.

title: PytorchVision
text: In essence, taking pixel values and building a model to find patterns in them to use on future pixel values.

title: PytorchVision
text: Plus, even for this small dataset (yes, even 60,000 images in deep learning is considered quite small), could you write a program to classify each one of them?

title: PytorchVision
text: You probably could.

title: PytorchVision
text: But I think coding a model in PyTorch would be faster.

title: PytorchVision
text: Question: Do you think the above data can be modeled with only straight (linear) lines? Or do you think you'd also need non-straight (non-linear) lines?

title: PytorchVision
text: Now we've got a dataset ready to go.

title: PytorchVision
text: The next step is to prepare it with a torch.utils.data.DataLoader or DataLoader for short.

title: PytorchVision
text: The DataLoader does what you think it might do.

title: PytorchVision
text: It helps load data into a model.

title: PytorchVision
text: For training and for inference.

title: PytorchVision
text: It turns a large Dataset into a Python iterable of smaller chunks.

title: PytorchVision
text: These smaller chunks are called batches or mini-batches and can be set by the batch_size parameter.

title: PytorchVision
text: Why do this?

title: PytorchVision
text: Because it's more computationally efficient.

title: PytorchVision
text: In an ideal world you could do the forward pass and backward pass across all of your data at once.

title: PytorchVision
text: But once you start using really large datasets, unless you've got infinite computing power, it's easier to break them up into batches.

title: PytorchVision
text: It also gives your model more opportunities to improve.

title: PytorchVision
text: With mini-batches (small portions of the data), gradient descent is performed more often per epoch (once per mini-batch rather than once per epoch).

title: PytorchVision
text: What's a good batch size?

title: PytorchVision
text: 32 is a good place to start for a fair amount of problems.

title: PytorchVision
text: But since this is a value you can set (a hyperparameter ) you can try all different kinds of values, though generally powers of 2 are used most often (e.g. 32, 64, 128, 256, 512).

title: PytorchVision
text: Batching FashionMNIST with a batch size of 32 and shuffle turned on. A similar batching process will occur for other datasets but will differ depending on the batch size.

title: PytorchVision
text: Let's create DataLoader 's for our training and test sets.

title: PytorchVision
text: from torch.utils.data import DataLoader # Setup the batch size hyperparameter BATCH_SIZE = 32 # Turn datasets into iterables (batches) train_dataloader = DataLoader ( train_data , # dataset to turn into iterable batch_size = BATCH_SIZE , # how many samples per batch? shuffle = True # shuffle data every epoch? ) test_dataloader = DataLoader ( test_data , batch_size = BATCH_SIZE , shuffle = False # don't necessarily have to shuffle the testing data ) # Let's check out what we've created print ( f "Dataloaders: { train_dataloader , test_dataloader } " ) print ( f "Length of train dataloader: { len ( train_dataloader ) } batches of { BATCH_SIZE } " ) print ( f "Length of test dataloader: { len ( test_dataloader ) } batches of { BATCH_SIZE } " )
