title: PytorchVision
text: Data loaded and prepared!

title: PytorchVision
text: Time to build a baseline model by subclassing nn.Module .

title: PytorchVision
text: A baseline model is one of the simplest models you can imagine.

title: PytorchVision
text: You use the baseline as a starting point and try to improve upon it with subsequent, more complicated models.

title: PytorchVision
text: Our baseline will consist of two nn.Linear() layers.

title: PytorchVision
text: We've done this in a previous section but there's going to be one slight difference.

title: PytorchVision
text: Because we're working with image data, we're going to use a different layer to start things off.

title: PytorchVision
text: And that's the nn.Flatten() layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: nn.Flatten() compresses the dimensions of a tensor into a single vector.

title: PytorchVision
text: This is easier to understand when you see it.

title: PytorchVision
text: # Create a flatten layer flatten_model = nn . Flatten () # all nn modules function as a model (can do a forward pass) # Get a single sample x = train_features_batch [ 0 ] # Flatten the sample output = flatten_model ( x ) # perform forward pass # Print out what happened print ( f "Shape before flattening: { x . shape } -> [color_channels, height, width]" ) print ( f "Shape after flattening: { output . shape } -> [color_channels, height*width]" ) # Try uncommenting below and see what happens #print(x) #print(output)

title: PytorchVision
text:
Shape before flattening: torch.Size([1, 28, 28]) -> [color_channels, height, width]
Shape after flattening: torch.Size([1, 784]) -> [color_channels, height*width]

title: PytorchVision
text: The nn.Flatten() layer took our shape from [color_channels, height, width] to [color_channels, height*width] .

title: PytorchVision
text: Why do this?

title: PytorchVision
text: Because we've now turned our pixel data from height and width dimensions into one long feature vector .

title: PytorchVision
text: And nn.Linear() layers like their inputs to be in the form of feature vectors.

title: PytorchVision
text: Let's create our first model using nn.Flatten() as the first layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: from torch import nn class FashionMNISTModelV0 ( nn . Module ): def __init__ ( self , input_shape : int , hidden_units : int , output_shape : int ): super () . __init__ () self . layer_stack = nn . Sequential ( nn . Flatten (), # neural networks like their inputs in vector form nn . Linear ( in_features = input_shape , out_features = hidden_units ), # in_features = number of features in a data sample (784 pixels) nn . Linear ( in_features = hidden_units , out_features = output_shape ) ) def forward ( self , x ): return self . layer_stack ( x )

title: PytorchVision
text: Wonderful!

title: PytorchVision
text: We've got a baseline model class we can use, now let's instantiate a model.

title: PytorchVision
text: We'll need to set the following parameters:

title: PytorchVision
text: input_shape=784 - this is how many features you've got going in the model, in our case, it's one for every pixel in the target image (28 pixels high by 28 pixels wide = 784 features).

title: PytorchVision
text: hidden_units=10 - number of units/neurons in the hidden layer(s), this number could be whatever you want but to keep the model small we'll start with 10 .

title: PytorchVision
text: output_shape=len(class_names) - since we're working with a multi-class classification problem, we need an output neuron per class in our dataset.

title: PytorchVision
text: Let's create an instance of our model and send to the CPU for now (we'll run a small test for running model_0 on CPU vs. a similar model on GPU soon).

title: PytorchVision
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Need to setup model with input parameters model_0 = FashionMNISTModelV0 ( input_shape = 784 , # one for every pixel (28x28) hidden_units = 10 , # how many units in the hidden layer output_shape = len ( class_names ) # one for every class ) model_0 . to ( "cpu" ) # keep model on CPU to begin with

title: PytorchVision
text:
FashionMNISTModelV0(
  (layer_stack): Sequential(
    (0): Flatten(start_dim=1, end_dim=-1)
    (1): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=10, bias=True)
    (2): Linear(in_features=10, out_features=10, bias=True)
  )
)

text: from timeit import default_timer as timer def print_train_time ( start : float , end : float , device : torch . device = None ): """Prints difference between start and end time. Args: start (float): Start time of computation (preferred in timeit format). end (float): End time of computation. device ([type], optional): Device that compute is running on. Defaults to None. Returns: float: time between start and end in seconds (higher is longer). """ total_time = end - start print ( f "Train time on { device } : { total_time : .3f } seconds" ) return total_time

text: The function will use the model to make predictions on the data in the DataLoader and then we can evaluate those predictions using the loss function and accuracy function.

section: 4. Make predictions and get Model 0 results
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) def eval_model ( model : torch . nn . Module , data_loader : torch . utils . data . DataLoader , loss_fn : torch . nn . Module , accuracy_fn ): """Returns a dictionary containing the results of model predicting on data_loader. Args: model (torch.nn.Module): A PyTorch model capable of making predictions on data_loader. data_loader (torch.utils.data.DataLoader): The target dataset to predict on. loss_fn (torch.nn.Module): The loss function of model. accuracy_fn: An accuracy function to compare the models predictions to the truth labels. Returns: (dict): Results of model making predictions on data_loader. """ loss , acc = 0 , 0 model . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): for X , y in data_loader : # Make predictions with the model y_pred = model ( X ) # Accumulate the loss and accuracy values per batch loss += loss_fn ( y_pred , y ) acc += accuracy_fn ( y_true = y , y_pred = y_pred . argmax ( dim = 1 )) # For accuracy, need the prediction labels (logits -> pred_prob -> pred_labels) # Scale loss and acc to find the average loss/acc per batch loss /= len ( data_loader ) acc /= len ( data_loader ) return { "model_name" : model . __class__ . __name__ , # only works when model was created with a class "model_loss" : loss . item (), "model_acc" : acc } # Calculate model 0 results on test dataset model_0_results = eval_model ( model = model_0 , data_loader = test_dataloader , loss_fn = loss_fn , accuracy_fn = accuracy_fn ) model_0_results

title: PytorchVision
text: For the training loop we'll create a function called train_step() which takes in a model, a DataLoader a loss function and an optimizer.

title: PytorchVision
text: The testing loop will be similar but it'll be called test_step() and it'll take in a model, a DataLoader , a loss function and an evaluation function.

title: PytorchVision
text: Note: Since these are functions, you can customize them in any way you like. What we're making here can be considered barebones training and testing functions for our specific classification use case.

title: PytorchVision
text: def train_step ( model : torch . nn . Module , data_loader : torch . utils . data . DataLoader , loss_fn : torch . nn . Module , optimizer : torch . optim . Optimizer , accuracy_fn , device : torch . device = device ): train_loss , train_acc = 0 , 0 model . to ( device ) for batch , ( X , y ) in enumerate ( data_loader ): # Send data to GPU X , y = X . to ( device ), y . to ( device ) # 1. Forward pass y_pred = model ( X ) # 2. Calculate loss loss = loss_fn ( y_pred , y ) train_loss += loss train_acc += accuracy_fn ( y_true = y , y_pred = y_pred . argmax ( dim = 1 )) # Go from logits -> pred labels # 3. Optimizer zero grad optimizer . zero_grad () # 4. Loss backward loss . backward () # 5. Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Calculate loss and accuracy per epoch and print out what's happening train_loss /= len ( data_loader ) train_acc /= len ( data_loader ) print ( f "Train loss: { train_loss : .5f } | Train accuracy: { train_acc : .2f } %" ) def test_step ( data_loader : torch . utils . data . DataLoader , model : torch . nn . Module , loss_fn : torch . nn . Module , accuracy_fn , device : torch . device = device ): test_loss , test_acc = 0 , 0 model . to ( device ) model . eval () # put model in eval mode # Turn on inference context manager with torch . inference_mode (): for X , y in data_loader : # Send data to GPU X , y = X . to ( device ), y . to ( device ) # 1. Forward pass test_pred = model ( X ) # 2. Calculate loss and accuracy test_loss += loss_fn ( test_pred , y ) test_acc += accuracy_fn ( y_true = y , y_pred = test_pred . argmax ( dim = 1 ) # Go from logits -> pred labels ) # Adjust metrics and print out test_loss /= len ( data_loader ) test_acc /= len ( data_loader ) print ( f "Test loss: { test_loss : .5f } | Test accuracy: { test_acc : .2f } % \n " )

title: PytorchVision
text: Question: "I used a GPU but my model didn't train faster, why might that be?"

title: PytorchVision
text: Answer: Well, one reason could be because your dataset and model are both so small (like the dataset and model we're working with) the benefits of using a GPU are outweighed by the time it actually takes to transfer the data there.

title: PytorchVision
text: There's a small bottleneck between copying data from the CPU memory (default) to the GPU memory.

title: PytorchVision
text: So for smaller models and datasets, the CPU might actually be the optimal place to compute on.

title: PytorchVision
text: But for larger datasets and models, the speed of computing the GPU can offer usually far outweighs the cost of getting the data there.

title: PytorchVision
text: However, this is largely dependent on the hardware you're using. With practice, you will get used to where the best place to train your models is.

title: PytorchVision
text: And then the thing you thought might not work does.

title: PytorchVision
text: It's part science, part art.

title: PytorchVision
text: From the looks of things, it seems like our model is overfitting on the training data.

title: PytorchVision
text: Overfitting means our model is learning the training data well but those patterns aren't generalizing to the testing data.

title: PytorchVision
text: Two of the main ways to fix overfitting include:

title: PytorchVision
text: Using a smaller or different model (some models fit certain kinds of data better than others).

title: PytorchVision
text: Using a larger dataset (the more data, the more chance a model has to learn generalizable patterns).

title: PytorchVision
text: There are more, but I'm going to leave that as a challenge for you to explore.

title: PytorchVision
text: Try searching online, "ways to prevent overfitting in machine learning" and see what comes up.

title: PytorchVision
text: In the meantime, let's take a look at number 1: using a different model.

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: Alright, time to step things up a notch.

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: It's time to create a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN or ConvNet).

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: CNN's are known for their capabilities to find patterns in visual data.

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: And since we're dealing with visual data, let's see if using a CNN model can improve upon our baseline.

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: The CNN model we're going to be using is known as TinyVGG from the CNN Explainer website.

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: It follows the typical structure of a convolutional neural network:

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: Input layer -> [Convolutional layer -> activation layer -> pooling layer] -> Output layer

title: PytorchVision
section: 7. Model 2: Building a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)
text: Where the contents of [Convolutional layer -> activation layer -> pooling layer] can be upscaled and repeated multiple times, depending on requirements.

title: PytorchVision
text: Question: Wait, you say CNN's are good for images, are there any other model types I should be aware of?

title: PytorchVision
text: Good question.

title: PytorchVision
text: This table is a good general guide for which model to use (though there are exceptions).

title: PytorchVision
text: Note: The table above is only for reference, the model you end up using will be highly dependent on the problem you're working on and the constraints you have (amount of data, latency requirements).

title: PytorchVision
text: Enough talking about models, let's now build a CNN that replicates the model on the CNN Explainer website .

title: PytorchVision
text: To do so, we'll leverage the nn.Conv2d() and nn.MaxPool2d() layers from torch.nn .

title: PytorchVision
text: # Create a convolutional neural network class FashionMNISTModelV2 ( nn . Module ): """ Model architecture copying TinyVGG from: https://poloclub.github.io/cnn-explainer/ """ def __init__ ( self , input_shape : int , hidden_units : int , output_shape : int ): super () . __init__ () self . block_1 = nn . Sequential ( nn . Conv2d ( in_channels = input_shape , out_channels = hidden_units , kernel_size = 3 , # how big is the square that's going over the image? stride = 1 , # default padding = 1 ), # options = "valid" (no padding) or "same" (output has same shape as input) or int for specific number nn . ReLU (), nn . Conv2d ( in_channels = hidden_units , out_channels = hidden_units , kernel_size = 3 , stride = 1 , padding = 1 ), nn . ReLU (), nn . MaxPool2d ( kernel_size = 2 , stride = 2 ) # default stride value is same as kernel_size ) self . block_2 = nn . Sequential ( nn . Conv2d ( hidden_units , hidden_units , 3 , padding = 1 ), nn . ReLU (), nn . Conv2d ( hidden_units , hidden_units , 3 , padding = 1 ), nn . ReLU (), nn . MaxPool2d ( 2 ) ) self . classifier = nn . Sequential ( nn . Flatten (), # Where did this in_features shape come from? # It's because each layer of our network compresses and changes the shape of our input data. nn . Linear ( in_features = hidden_units * 7 * 7 , out_features = output_shape ) ) def forward ( self , x : torch . Tensor ): x = self . block_1 ( x ) # print(x.shape) x = self . block_2 ( x ) # print(x.shape) x = self . classifier ( x ) # print(x.shape) return x torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) model_2 = FashionMNISTModelV2 ( input_shape = 1 , hidden_units = 10 , output_shape = len ( class_names )) . to ( device ) model_2

title: PytorchVision
text:
FashionMNISTModelV2(
  (block_1): Sequential(
    (0): Conv2d(1, 10, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    (1): ReLU()
    (2): Conv2d(10, 10, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    (3): ReLU()
    (4): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
  )
  (block_2): Sequential(
    (0): Conv2d(10, 10, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    (1): ReLU()
    (2): Conv2d(10, 10, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1))
    (3): ReLU()
    (4): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
  )
  (classifier): Sequential(
    (0): Flatten(start_dim=1, end_dim=-1)
    (1): Linear(in_features=490, out_features=10, bias=True)
  )
)

title: PytorchVision

title: PytorchVision

title: PytorchVision
text: We could start using our model above and see what happens but let's first step through the two new layers we've added:

title: PytorchVision
text: nn.Conv2d() , also known as a convolutional layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: nn.MaxPool2d() , also known as a max pooling layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: Question: What does the "2d" in nn.Conv2d() stand for?

title: PytorchVision
text: The 2d is for 2-dimensional data. As in, our images have two dimensions: height and width. Yes, there's color channel dimension but each of the color channel dimensions have two dimensions too: height and width.

title: PytorchVision
text: For other dimensional data (such as 1D for text or 3D for 3D objects) there's also nn.Conv1d() and nn.Conv3d() .

title: PytorchVision
text: To test the layers out, let's create some toy data just like the data used on CNN Explainer.

title: PytorchVision
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Create sample batch of random numbers with same size as image batch images = torch . randn ( size = ( 32 , 3 , 64 , 64 )) # [batch_size, color_channels, height, width] test_image = images [ 0 ] # get a single image for testing print ( f "Image batch shape: { images . shape } -> [batch_size, color_channels, height, width]" ) print ( f "Single image shape: { test_image . shape } -> [color_channels, height, width]" ) print ( f "Single image pixel values: \n { test_image } " )

title: PytorchVision
text: Let's create an example nn.Conv2d() with various parameters:

title: PytorchVision
text: in_channels (int) - Number of channels in the input image.

title: PytorchVision
text: out_channels (int) - Number of channels produced by the convolution.

title: PytorchVision
text: kernel_size (int or tuple) - Size of the convolving kernel/filter.

title: PytorchVision
text: stride (int or tuple, optional) - How big of a step the convolving kernel takes at a time. Default: 1.

title: PytorchVision
text: padding (int, tuple, str) - Padding added to all four sides of input. Default: 0.

title: PytorchVision
text: Example of what happens when you change the hyperparameters of a nn.Conv2d() layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Create a convolutional layer with same dimensions as TinyVGG # (try changing any of the parameters and see what happens) conv_layer = nn . Conv2d ( in_channels = 3 , out_channels = 10 , kernel_size = 3 , stride = 1 , padding = 0 ) # also try using "valid" or "same" here # Pass the data through the convolutional layer conv_layer ( test_image ) # Note: If running PyTorch <1.11.0, this will error because of shape issues (nn.Conv.2d() expects a 4d tensor as input)

title: PytorchVision
text: If we try to pass a single image in, we get a shape mismatch error:

title: PytorchVision
text: RuntimeError: Expected 4-dimensional input for 4-dimensional weight [10, 3, 3, 3], but got 3-dimensional input of size [3, 64, 64] instead

title: PytorchVision
text: Note: If you're running PyTorch 1.11.0+, this error won't occur.

title: PytorchVision
text: This is because our nn.Conv2d() layer expects a 4-dimensional tensor as input with size (N, C, H, W) or [batch_size, color_channels, height, width] .

title: PytorchVision
text: Right now our single image test_image only has a shape of [color_channels, height, width] or [3, 64, 64] .

title: PytorchVision
text: We can fix this for a single image using test_image.unsqueeze(dim=0) to add an extra dimension for N .

title: PytorchVision
text: # Add extra dimension to test image test_image . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 ) . shape

title: PytorchVision
text: # Pass test image with extra dimension through conv_layer conv_layer ( test_image . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 )) . shape

title: PytorchVision
text: Hmm, notice what happens to our shape (the same shape as the first layer of TinyVGG on CNN Explainer ), we get different channel sizes as well as different pixel sizes.

title: PytorchVision
text: What if we changed the values of conv_layer ?

title: PytorchVision
text: torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Create a new conv_layer with different values (try setting these to whatever you like) conv_layer_2 = nn . Conv2d ( in_channels = 3 , # same number of color channels as our input image out_channels = 10 , kernel_size = ( 5 , 5 ), # kernel is usually a square so a tuple also works stride = 2 , padding = 0 ) # Pass single image through new conv_layer_2 (this calls nn.Conv2d()'s forward() method on the input) conv_layer_2 ( test_image . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 )) . shape

title: PytorchVision
text: Woah, we get another shape change.

title: PytorchVision
text: Now our image is of shape [1, 10, 30, 30] (it will be different if you use different values) or [batch_size=1, color_channels=10, height=30, width=30] .

title: PytorchVision
text: What's going on here?

title: PytorchVision
text: Behind the scenes, our nn.Conv2d() is compressing the information stored in the image.

title: PytorchVision
text: It does this by performing operations on the input (our test image) against its internal parameters.

title: PytorchVision
text: The goal of this is similar to all of the other neural networks we've been building.

title: PytorchVision
text: Data goes in and the layers try to update their internal parameters (patterns) to lower the loss function thanks to some help of the optimizer.

title: PytorchVision
text: The only difference is how the different layers calculate their parameter updates or in PyTorch terms, the operation present in the layer forward() method.

title: PytorchVision
text: If we check out our conv_layer_2.state_dict() we'll find a similar weight and bias setup as we've seen before.

title: PytorchVision
text: # Check out the conv_layer_2 internal parameters print ( conv_layer_2 . state_dict ())

title: PytorchVision
text: Look at that! A bunch of random numbers for a weight and bias tensor.

title: PytorchVision
text: The shapes of these are manipulated by the inputs we passed to nn.Conv2d() when we set it up.

title: PytorchVision
text: Let's check them out.

title: PytorchVision
text:
# Get shapes of weight and bias tensors within conv_layer_2 print ( f "conv_layer_2 weight shape: 
 { conv_layer_2 . weight . shape } -> [out_channels=10, in_channels=3, kernel_size=5, kernel_size=5]" ) print ( f " 
 conv_layer_2 bias shape: 
 { conv_layer_2 . bias . shape } -> [out_channels=10]" )

title: PytorchVision
text:
conv_layer_2 weight shape: 
torch.Size([10, 3, 5, 5]) -> [out_channels=10, in_channels=3, kernel_size=5, kernel_size=5]

conv_layer_2 bias shape: 
torch.Size([10]) -> [out_channels=10]

title: PytorchVision
text: Question: What should we set the parameters of our nn.Conv2d() layers?

title: PytorchVision
text: That's a good one. But similar to many other things in machine learning, the values of these aren't set in stone (and recall, because these values are ones we can set ourselves, they're referred to as " hyperparameters ").

title: PytorchVision
text: The best way to find out is to try out different values and see how they effect your model's performance.

title: PytorchVision
text: Or even better, find a working example on a problem similar to yours (like we've done with TinyVGG) and copy it.

title: PytorchVision
text: We're working with a different of layer here to what we've seen before.

title: PytorchVision
text: But the premise remains the same: start with random numbers and update them to better represent the data.

title: PytorchVision
text: Now let's check out what happens when we move data through nn.MaxPool2d() .

title: PytorchVision
text: # Print out original image shape without and with unsqueezed dimension print ( f "Test image original shape: { test_image . shape } " ) print ( f "Test image with unsqueezed dimension: { test_image . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 ) . shape } " ) # Create a sample nn.MaxPoo2d() layer max_pool_layer = nn . MaxPool2d ( kernel_size = 2 ) # Pass data through just the conv_layer test_image_through_conv = conv_layer ( test_image . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 )) print ( f "Shape after going through conv_layer(): { test_image_through_conv . shape } " ) # Pass data through the max pool layer test_image_through_conv_and_max_pool = max_pool_layer ( test_image_through_conv ) print ( f "Shape after going through conv_layer() and max_pool_layer(): { test_image_through_conv_and_max_pool . shape } " )

title: PytorchVision
text:
Test image original shape: torch.Size([3, 64, 64])
Test image with unsqueezed dimension: torch.Size([1, 3, 64, 64])
Shape after going through conv_layer(): torch.Size([1, 10, 62, 62])
Shape after going through conv_layer() and max_pool_layer(): torch.Size([1, 10, 31, 31])

title: PytorchVision
text: Notice the change in the shapes of what's happening in and out of a nn.MaxPool2d() layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: The kernel_size of the nn.MaxPool2d() layer will affect the size of the output shape.

title: PytorchVision
text: In our case, the shape halves from a 62x62 image to 31x31 image.

title: PytorchVision
text: Let's see this work with a smaller tensor.

title: PytorchVision
text:
torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Create a random tensor with a similar number of dimensions to our images random_tensor = torch . randn ( size = ( 1 , 1 , 2 , 2 )) print ( f "Random tensor: 
 { random_tensor } " ) print ( f "Random tensor shape: { random_tensor . shape } " ) # Create a max pool layer max_pool_layer = nn . MaxPool2d ( kernel_size = 2 ) # see what happens when you change the kernel_size value # Pass the random tensor through the max pool layer max_pool_tensor = max_pool_layer ( random_tensor ) print ( f " 
 Max pool tensor: 
 { max_pool_tensor } <- this is the maximum value from random_tensor" ) print ( f "Max pool tensor shape: { max_pool_tensor . shape } " )

title: PytorchVision
text:
Random tensor:
tensor([[[[0.3367, 0.1288],
          [0.2345, 0.2303]]]])
Random tensor shape: torch.Size([1, 1, 2, 2])

Max pool tensor:
tensor([[[[0.3367]]]]) <- this is the maximum value from random_tensor
Max pool tensor shape: torch.Size([1, 1, 1, 1])

title: PytorchVision
text: Notice the final two dimensions between random_tensor and max_pool_tensor , they go from [2, 2] to [1, 1] .

title: PytorchVision
text: In essence, they get halved.

title: PytorchVision
text: And the change would be different for different values of kernel_size for nn.MaxPool2d() .

title: PytorchVision
text: Also notice the value leftover in max_pool_tensor is the maximum value from random_tensor .

title: PytorchVision
text: What's happening here?

title: PytorchVision
text: This is another important piece of the puzzle of neural networks.

title: PytorchVision
text: Essentially, every layer in a neural network is trying to compress data from higher dimensional space to lower dimensional space .

title: PytorchVision
text: In other words, take a lot of numbers (raw data) and learn patterns in those numbers, patterns that are predictive whilst also being smaller in size than the original values.

title: PytorchVision
text: From an artificial intelligence perspective, you could consider the whole goal of a neural network to compress information.

title: PytorchVision
text: This means, that from the point of view of a neural network, intelligence is compression.

title: PytorchVision
text: This is the idea of the use of a nn.MaxPool2d() layer: take the maximum value from a portion of a tensor and disregard the rest.

title: PytorchVision
text: In essence, lowering the dimensionality of a tensor whilst still retaining a (hopefully) significant portion of the information.

title: PytorchVision
text: It is the same story for a nn.Conv2d() layer.

title: PytorchVision
text: Except instead of just taking the maximum, the nn.Conv2d() performs a convolutional operation on the data (see this in action on the CNN Explainer webpage ).

title: PytorchVision
text: Something to be aware of in machine learning is the performance-speed tradeoff.

title: PytorchVision
text: Generally, you get better performance out of a larger, more complex model (like we did with model_2 ).

title: PytorchVision
text: However, this performance increase often comes at a sacrifice of training speed and inference speed.

title: PytorchVision
text: Note: The training times you get will be very dependent on the hardware you use.

title: PytorchVision
text: Generally, the more CPU cores you have, the faster your models will train on CPU. And similar for GPUs.

title: PytorchVision
text: Newer hardware (in terms of age) will also often train models faster due to incorporating technological advances.

Module , data : list , device : torch . device = device ): pred_probs = [] model . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): for sample in data : # Prepare sample sample = torch . unsqueeze ( sample , dim = 0 ) . to ( device ) # Add an extra dimension and send sample to device # Forward pass (model outputs raw logit) pred_logit = model ( sample ) # Get prediction probability (logit -> prediction probability) pred_prob = torch . softmax ( pred_logit . squeeze (), dim = 0 ) # note: perform softmax on the "logits" dimension, not "batch" dimension (in this case we have a batch size of 1, so can perform on dim=0) # Get pred_prob off GPU for further calculations pred_probs . append ( pred_prob . cpu ()) # Stack the pred_probs to turn list into a tensor return torch . stack ( pred_probs )

title: CustomDatasets
text: In the last notebook, notebook 03 , we looked at how to build computer vision models on an in-built dataset in PyTorch (FashionMNIST).

title: CustomDatasets
text: The steps we took are similar across many different problems in machine learning.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Find a dataset, turn the dataset into numbers, build a model (or find an existing model) to find patterns in those numbers that can be used for prediction.

title: CustomDatasets
text: PyTorch has many built-in datasets used for a wide number of machine learning benchmarks, however, you'll often want to use your own custom dataset .

title: CustomDatasets
text: A custom dataset is a collection of data relating to a specific problem you're working on.

title: CustomDatasets
text: In essence, a custom dataset can be comprised of almost anything.

title: CustomDatasets
text: For example, if we were building a food image classification app like Nutrify , our custom dataset might be images of food.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Or if we were trying to build a model to classify whether or not a text-based review on a website was positive or negative, our custom dataset might be examples of existing customer reviews and their ratings.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Or if we were trying to build a sound classification app, our custom dataset might be sound samples alongside their sample labels.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Or if we were trying to build a recommendation system for customers purchasing things on our website, our custom dataset might be examples of products other people have bought.

title: CustomDatasets
text: PyTorch includes many existing functions to load in various custom datasets in the TorchVision , TorchText , TorchAudio and TorchRec domain libraries.

title: CustomDatasets
text: But sometimes these existing functions may not be enough.

title: CustomDatasets
text: In that case, we can always subclass torch.utils.data.Dataset and customize it to our liking.

title: CustomDatasets
text: We're going to be applying the PyTorch Workflow we covered in notebook 01 and notebook 02 to a computer vision problem.

title: CustomDatasets
text: But instead of using an in-built PyTorch dataset, we're going to be using our own dataset of pizza, steak and sushi images.

title: CustomDatasets
text: The goal will be to load these images and then build a model to train and predict on them.

title: CustomDatasets
text: What we're going to build. We'll use torchvision.datasets as well as our own custom Dataset class to load in images of food and then we'll build a PyTorch computer vision model to hopefully be able to classify them.

title: CustomDatasets
text: There are several different kinds of pre-built datasets and dataset loaders for PyTorch, depending on the problem you're working on.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Since we're working with a vision problem, we'll be looking at torchvision.datasets for our data loading functions as well as torchvision.transforms for preparing our data.

title: CustomDatasets

title: CustomDatasets
text: import torch from torch.utils.data import DataLoader from torchvision import datasets , transforms

title: CustomDatasets
text: We've got folders of images but before we can use them with PyTorch, we need to convert them into tensors.

title: CustomDatasets
text: One of the ways we can do this is by using the torchvision.transforms module.

title: CustomDatasets
text: torchvision.transforms contains many pre-built methods for formatting images, turning them into tensors and even manipulating them for data augmentation (the practice of altering data to make it harder for a model to learn, we'll see this later on) purposes .

title: CustomDatasets
text: To get experience with torchvision.transforms , let's write a series of transform steps that:

title: CustomDatasets
text: Resize the images using transforms.Resize() (from about 512x512 to 64x64, the same shape as the images on the CNN Explainer website ).

title: CustomDatasets
text: Flip our images randomly on the horizontal using transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip() (this could be considered a form of data augmentation because it will artificially change our image data).

title: CustomDatasets
text: Turn our images from a PIL image to a PyTorch tensor using transforms.ToTensor() .

title: CustomDatasets
text: We can compile all of these steps using torchvision.transforms.Compose() .

title: CustomDatasets
text: # Write transform for image data_transform = transforms . Compose ([ # Resize the images to 64x64 transforms . Resize ( size = ( 64 , 64 )), # Flip the images randomly on the horizontal transforms . RandomHorizontalFlip ( p = 0.5 ), # p = probability of flip, 0.5 = 50% chance # Turn the image into a torch.Tensor transforms . ToTensor () # this also converts all pixel values from 0 to 255 to be between 0.0 and 1.0 ])

title: CustomDatasets
text: Now we've got a composition of transforms, let's write a function to try them out on various images.

title: CustomDatasets
text: def plot_transformed_images ( image_paths , transform , n = 3 , seed = 42 ): """Plots a series of random images from image_paths. Will open n image paths from image_paths, transform them with transform and plot them side by side. Args: image_paths (list): List of target image paths. transform (PyTorch Transforms): Transforms to apply to images. n (int, optional): Number of images to plot. Defaults to 3. seed (int, optional): Random seed for the random generator. Defaults to 42. """ random . seed ( seed ) random_image_paths = random . sample ( image_paths , k = n ) for image_path in random_image_paths : with Image . open ( image_path ) as f : fig , ax = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 ) ax [ 0 ] . imshow ( f ) ax [ 0 ] . set_title ( f "Original \n Size: { f . size } " ) ax [ 0 ] . axis ( "off" ) # Transform and plot image # Note: permute() will change shape of image to suit matplotlib # (PyTorch default is [C, H, W] but Matplotlib is [H, W, C]) transformed_image = transform ( f ) . permute ( 1 , 2 , 0 ) ax [ 1 ] . imshow ( transformed_image ) ax [ 1 ] . set_title ( f "Transformed \n Size: { transformed_image . shape } " ) ax [ 1 ] . axis ( "off" ) fig . suptitle ( f "Class: { image_path . parent . stem } " , fontsize = 16 ) plot_transformed_images ( image_path_list , transform = data_transform , n = 3 )

title: CustomDatasets
text: Nice!

title: CustomDatasets
text: We've now got a way to convert our images to tensors using torchvision.transforms .

title: CustomDatasets
text: We also manipulate their size and orientation if needed (some models prefer images of different sizes and shapes).

title: CustomDatasets
text: Generally, the larger the shape of the image, the more information a model can recover.

title: CustomDatasets
text: For example, an image of size [256, 256, 3] will have 16x more pixels than an image of size [64, 64, 3] ( (256*256*3)/(64*64*3)=16 ).

title: CustomDatasets
text: However, the tradeoff is that more pixels requires more computations.

section: 5.1 Creating a helper function to get class names
text: # Make function to find classes in target directory def find_classes ( directory : str ) -> Tuple [ List [ str ], Dict [ str , int ]]: """Finds the class folder names in a target directory. Assumes target directory is in standard image classification format. Args: directory (str): target directory to load classnames from. Returns: Tuple[List[str], Dict[str, int]]: (list_of_class_names, dict(class_name: idx...)) Example: find_classes("food_images/train") >>> (["class_1", "class_2"], {"class_1": 0, ...}) """ # 1. Get the class names by scanning the target directory classes = sorted ( entry . name for entry in os . scandir ( directory ) if entry . is_dir ()) # 2. Raise an error if class names not found if not classes : raise FileNotFoundError ( f "Couldn't find any classes in { directory } ." ) # 3. Create a dictionary of index labels (computers prefer numerical rather than string labels) class_to_idx = { cls_name : i for i , cls_name in enumerate ( classes )} return classes , class_to_idx

text: Overwrite the __len__ method of torch.utils.data.Dataset to return the number of samples in the Dataset , this is recommended but not required. This is so you can call len(Dataset) .

title: CustomDatasets

text: Overwrite the __getitem__ method of torch.utils.data.Dataset to return a single sample from the Dataset , this is required.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 5.2 Create a custom Dataset to replicate ImageFolder
text: Let's do it!

title: CustomDatasets
section: 5.2 Create a custom Dataset to replicate ImageFolder
text: # Write a custom dataset class (inherits from torch.utils.data.Dataset) from torch.utils.data import Dataset # 1. Subclass torch.utils.data.Dataset class ImageFolderCustom ( Dataset ): # 2. Initialize with a targ_dir and transform (optional) parameter def __init__ ( self , targ_dir : str , transform = None ) -> None : # 3. Create class attributes # Get all image paths self . paths = list ( pathlib . Path ( targ_dir ) . glob ( "*/*.jpg" )) # note: you'd have to update this if you've got .png's or .jpeg's # Setup transforms self . transform = transform # Create classes and class_to_idx attributes self . classes , self . class_to_idx = find_classes ( targ_dir ) # 4. Make function to load images def load_image ( self , index : int ) -> Image . Image : "Opens an image via a path and returns it." image_path = self . paths [ index ] return Image . open ( image_path ) # 5. Overwrite the __len__() method (optional but recommended for subclasses of torch.utils.data.Dataset) def __len__ ( self ) -> int : "Returns the total number of samples." return len ( self . paths ) # 6. Overwrite the __getitem__() method (required for subclasses of torch.utils.data.Dataset) def __getitem__ ( self , index : int ) -> Tuple [ torch . Tensor , int ]: "Returns one sample of data, data and label (X, y)." img = self . load_image ( index ) class_name = self . paths [ index ] . parent . name # expects path in data_folder/class_name/image.jpeg class_idx = self . class_to_idx [ class_name ] # Transform if necessary if self . transform : return self . transform ( img ), class_idx # return data, label (X, y) else : return img , class_idx # return data, label (X, y)

text: # 1. Take in a Dataset as well as a list of class names def display_random_images ( dataset : torch . utils . data . dataset . Dataset , classes : List [ str ] = None , n : int = 10 , display_shape : bool = True , seed : int = None ): # 2. Adjust display if n too high if n > 10 : n = 10 display_shape = False print ( f "For display purposes, n shouldn't be larger than 10, setting to 10 and removing shape display." ) # 3. Set random seed if seed : random . seed ( seed ) # 4. Get random sample indexes random_samples_idx = random . sample ( range ( len ( dataset )), k = n ) # 5. Setup plot plt . figure ( figsize = ( 16 , 8 )) # 6. Loop through samples and display random samples for i , targ_sample in enumerate ( random_samples_idx ): targ_image , targ_label = dataset [ targ_sample ][ 0 ], dataset [ targ_sample ][ 1 ] # 7. Adjust image tensor shape for plotting: [color_channels, height, width] -> [color_channels, height, width] targ_image_adjust = targ_image . permute ( 1 , 2 , 0 ) # Plot adjusted samples plt . subplot ( 1 , n , i + 1 ) plt . imshow ( targ_image_adjust ) plt . axis ( "off" ) if classes : title = f "class: { classes [ targ_label ] } " if display_shape : title = title + f " \n shape: { targ_image_adjust . shape } " plt . title ( title )

text: Let's now take a look at some other forms of data transforms.

title: CustomDatasets
text: We've seen a couple of transforms on our data already but there's plenty more.

title: CustomDatasets
text: You can see them all in the torchvision.transforms documentation .

title: CustomDatasets
text: The purpose of tranforms is to alter your images in some way.

title: CustomDatasets
text: That may be turning your images into a tensor (as we've seen before).

title: CustomDatasets
text: Or cropping it or randomly erasing a portion or randomly rotating them.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Doing these kinds of transforms is often referred to as data augmentation .

title: CustomDatasets
text: Data augmentation is the process of altering your data in such a way that you artificially increase the diversity of your training set.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Training a model on this artificially altered dataset hopefully results in a model that is capable of better generalization (the patterns it learns are more robust to future unseen examples).

title: CustomDatasets
text: You can see many different examples of data augmentation performed on images using torchvision.transforms in PyTorch's Illustration of Transforms example .

title: CustomDatasets
text: But let's try one out ourselves.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Machine learning is all about harnessing the power of randomness and research shows that random transforms (like transforms.RandAugment() and transforms.TrivialAugmentWide() ) generally perform better than hand-picked transforms.

title: CustomDatasets
text: The idea behind TrivialAugment is... well, trivial.

title: CustomDatasets
text: You have a set of transforms and you randomly pick a number of them to perform on an image and at a random magnitude between a given range (a higher magnitude means more instense).

title: CustomDatasets
text: The PyTorch team even used TrivialAugment it to train their latest state-of-the-art vision models .

title: CustomDatasets
text: TrivialAugment was one of the ingredients used in a recent state of the art training upgrade to various PyTorch vision models.

title: CustomDatasets
text: How about we test it out on some of our own images?

title: CustomDatasets
text: The main parameter to pay attention to in transforms.TrivialAugmentWide() is num_magnitude_bins=31 .

title: CustomDatasets
text: It defines how much of a range an intensity value will be picked to apply a certain transform, 0 being no range and 31 being maximum range (highest chance for highest intensity).

title: CustomDatasets
text: We can incorporate transforms.TrivialAugmentWide() into transforms.Compose() .

title: CustomDatasets
text: from torchvision import transforms train_transforms = transforms . Compose ([ transforms . Resize (( 224 , 224 )), transforms . TrivialAugmentWide ( num_magnitude_bins = 31 ), # how intense transforms . ToTensor () # use ToTensor() last to get everything between 0 & 1 ]) # Don't need to perform augmentation on the test data test_transforms = transforms . Compose ([ transforms . Resize (( 224 , 224 )), transforms . ToTensor () ])

title: CustomDatasets
text: Note: You usually don't perform data augmentation on the test set. The idea of data augmentation is to to artificially increase the diversity of the training set to better predict on the testing set.

title: CustomDatasets
text: However, you do need to make sure your test set images are transformed to tensors. We size the test images to the same size as our training images too, however, inference can be done on different size images if necessary (though this may alter performance).

title: CustomDatasets
text: Beautiful, now we've got a training transform (with data augmentation) and test transform (without data augmentation).

title: CustomDatasets
text: Let's test our data augmentation out!

text: Now let's make some training and test loop functions to train our model on the training data and evaluate our model on the testing data.

title: CustomDatasets
text: And to make sure we can use these the training and testing loops again, we'll functionize them.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Specifically, we're going to make three functions:

title: CustomDatasets
text: train_step() - takes in a model, a DataLoader , a loss function and an optimizer and trains the model on the DataLoader .

title: CustomDatasets
text: test_step() - takes in a model, a DataLoader and a loss function and evaluates the model on the DataLoader .

title: CustomDatasets
text: train() - performs 1. and 2. together for a given number of epochs and returns a results dictionary.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Note: We covered the steps in a PyTorch opimization loop in notebook 01 , as well as the Unofficial PyTorch Optimization Loop Song and we've built similar functions in notebook 03 .

title: CustomDatasets
text: Let's start by building train_step() .

title: CustomDatasets
text: Because we're dealing with batches in the DataLoader 's, we'll accumulate the model loss and accuracy values during training (by adding them up for each batch) and then adjust them at the end before we return them.

title: CustomDatasets
text: def train_step ( model : torch . nn . Module , dataloader : torch . utils . data . DataLoader , loss_fn : torch . nn . Module , optimizer : torch . optim . Optimizer ): # Put model in train mode model . train () # Setup train loss and train accuracy values train_loss , train_acc = 0 , 0 # Loop through data loader data batches for batch , ( X , y ) in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Send data to target device X , y = X . to ( device ), y . to ( device ) # 1. Forward pass y_pred = model ( X ) # 2. Calculate  and accumulate loss loss = loss_fn ( y_pred , y ) train_loss += loss . item () # 3. Optimizer zero grad optimizer . zero_grad () # 4. Loss backward loss . backward () # 5. Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Calculate and accumulate accuracy metrics across all batches y_pred_class = torch . argmax ( torch . softmax ( y_pred , dim = 1 ), dim = 1 ) train_acc += ( y_pred_class == y ) . sum () . item () / len ( y_pred ) # Adjust metrics to get average loss and accuracy per batch train_loss = train_loss / len ( dataloader ) train_acc = train_acc / len ( dataloader ) return train_loss , train_acc

title: CustomDatasets
text: Woohoo! train_step() function done.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Now let's do the same for the test_step() function.

title: CustomDatasets
text: The main difference here will be the test_step() won't take in an optimizer and therefore won't perform gradient descent.

title: CustomDatasets
text: But since we'll be doing inference, we'll make sure to turn on the torch.inference_mode() context manager for making predictions.

title: CustomDatasets
text: def test_step ( model : torch . nn . Module , dataloader : torch . utils . data . DataLoader , loss_fn : torch . nn . Module ): # Put model in eval mode model . eval () # Setup test loss and test accuracy values test_loss , test_acc = 0 , 0 # Turn on inference context manager with torch . inference_mode (): # Loop through DataLoader batches for batch , ( X , y ) in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Send data to target device X , y = X . to ( device ), y . to ( device ) # 1. Forward pass test_pred_logits = model ( X ) # 2. Calculate and accumulate loss loss = loss_fn ( test_pred_logits , y ) test_loss += loss . item () # Calculate and accumulate accuracy test_pred_labels = test_pred_logits . argmax ( dim = 1 ) test_acc += (( test_pred_labels == y ) . sum () . item () / len ( test_pred_labels )) # Adjust metrics to get average loss and accuracy per batch test_loss = test_loss / len ( dataloader ) test_acc = test_acc / len ( dataloader ) return test_loss , test_acc

section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: Looking at training and test loss curves is a great way to see if your model is overfitting .

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: An overfitting model is one that performs better (often by a considerable margin) on the training set than the validation/test set.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: If your training loss is far lower than your test loss, your model is overfitting .

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: As in, it's learning the patterns in the training too well and those patterns aren't generalizing to the test data.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: The other side is when your training and test loss are not as low as you'd like, this is considered underfitting .

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: The ideal position for a training and test loss curve is for them to line up closely with each other.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8. What should an ideal loss curve look like?
text: Left: If your training and test loss curves aren't as low as you'd like, this is considered underfitting . *Middle: When your test/validation loss is higher than your training loss this is considered overfitting . Right: The ideal scenario is when your training and test loss curves line up over time. This means your model is generalizing well. There are more combinations and different things loss curves can do, for more on these, see Google's Interpreting Loss Curves guide .*

title: CustomDatasets
text: Since the main problem with overfitting is that your model is fitting the training data too well , you'll want to use techniques to "reign it in".

title: CustomDatasets
text: A common technique of preventing overfitting is known as regularization .

title: CustomDatasets
text: I like to think of this as "making our models more regular", as in, capable of fitting more kinds of data.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Let's discuss a few methods to prevent overfitting.

title: CustomDatasets
text: There are more methods for dealing with overfitting but these are some of the main ones.

title: CustomDatasets
text: As you start to build more and more deep models, you'll find because deep learnings are so good at learning patterns in data, dealing with overfitting is one of the primary problems of deep learning.

title: CustomDatasets
text: When a model is underfitting it is considered to have poor predictive power on the training and test sets.

title: CustomDatasets
text: In essence, an underfitting model will fail to reduce the loss values to a desired level.

title: CustomDatasets
text: Right now, looking at our current loss curves, I'd considered our TinyVGG model, model_0 , to be underfitting the data.

title: CustomDatasets
text: The main idea behind dealing with underfitting is to increase your model's predictive power.

title: CustomDatasets
text: There are several ways to do this.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: None of the methods discussed above are silver bullets, meaning, they don't always work.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: And preventing overfitting and underfitting is possibly the most active area of machine learning research.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: Since everyone wants their models to fit better (less underfitting) but not so good they don't generalize well and perform in the real world (less overfitting).

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: There's a fine line between overfitting and underfitting.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: Because too much of each can cause the other.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: Transfer learning is perhaps one of the most powerful techniques when it comes to dealing with both overfitting and underfitting on your own problems.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 8.3 The balance between overfitting and underfitting
text: Rather than handcraft different overfitting and underfitting techniques, transfer learning enables you to take an already working model in a similar problem space to yours (say one from paperswithcode.com/sota or Hugging Face models ) and apply it to your own dataset.

section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: If you've trained a model on a certain dataset, chances are you'd like to make a prediction on your own custom data.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: In our case, since we've trained a model on pizza, steak and sushi images, how could we use our model to make a prediction on one of our own images?

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: To do so, we can load an image and then preprocess it in a way that matches the type of data our model was trained on .

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: In other words, we'll have to convert our own custom image to a tensor and make sure it's in the right datatype before passing it to our model.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: Let's start by downloading a custom image.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: Since our model predicts whether an image contains pizza, steak or sushi, let's download a photo of my Dad giving two thumbs up to a big pizza from the Learn PyTorch for Deep Learning GitHub .

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: We download the image using Python's requests module.

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11. Make a prediction on a custom image
text: Note: If you're using Google Colab, you can also upload an image to the current session by going to the left hand side menu -> Files -> Upload to session storage. Beware though, this image will delete when your Google Colab session ends.

text: Note: What we've just gone through are three of the classical and most common deep learning and PyTorch issues:

title: CustomDatasets

text: Wrong datatypes - our model expects torch.float32 where our original custom image was uint8 .

title: CustomDatasets

title: CustomDatasets
section: 11.2 Predicting on custom images with a trained PyTorch model
text: Wrong shapes - our model expected an input image of shape [N, C, H, W] or [batch_size, color_channels, height, width] whereas our custom image tensor was of shape [color_channels, height, width] .

text: def pred_and_plot_image ( model : torch . nn . Module , image_path : str , class_names : List [ str ] = None , transform = None , device : torch . device = device ): """Makes a prediction on a target image and plots the image with its prediction.""" # 1. Load in image and convert the tensor values to float32 target_image = torchvision . io . read_image ( str ( image_path )) . type ( torch . float32 ) # 2. Divide the image pixel values by 255 to get them between [0, 1] target_image = target_image / 255. # 3. Transform if necessary if transform : target_image = transform ( target_image ) # 4. Make sure the model is on the target device model . to ( device ) # 5. Turn on model evaluation mode and inference mode model . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): # Add an extra dimension to the image target_image = target_image . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 ) # Make a prediction on image with an extra dimension and send it to the target device target_image_pred = model ( target_image . to ( device )) # 6. Convert logits -> prediction probabilities (using torch.softmax() for multi-class classification) target_image_pred_probs = torch . softmax ( target_image_pred , dim = 1 ) # 7. Convert prediction probabilities -> prediction labels target_image_pred_label = torch . argmax ( target_image_pred_probs , dim = 1 ) # 8. Plot the image alongside the prediction and prediction probability plt . imshow ( target_image . squeeze () . permute ( 1 , 2 , 0 )) # make sure it's the right size for matplotlib if class_names : title = f "Pred: { class_names [ target_image_pred_label . cpu ()] } | Prob: { target_image_pred_probs . max () . cpu () : .3f } " else : title = f "Pred: { target_image_pred_label } | Prob: { target_image_pred_probs . max () . cpu () : .3f } " plt . title ( title ) plt . axis ( False );

title: TransferLearning
text: Note: This notebook uses torchvision 's new multi-weight support API (available in torchvision v0.13+) .

title: TransferLearning
text: We've built a few models by hand so far.

title: TransferLearning
text: But their performance has been poor.

title: TransferLearning
text: You might be thinking, is there a well-performing model that already exists for our problem?

title: TransferLearning
text: And in the world of deep learning, the answer is often yes .

title: TransferLearning
text: We'll see how by using a powerful technique called transfer learning .

title: TransferLearning
text: Transfer learning allows us to take the patterns (also called weights) another model has learned from another problem and use them for our own problem.

title: TransferLearning
text: For example, we can take the patterns a computer vision model has learned from datasets such as ImageNet (millions of images of different objects) and use them to power our FoodVision Mini model.

title: TransferLearning
text: Or we could take the patterns from a language model (a model that's been through large amounts of text to learn a representation of language) and use them as the basis of a model to classify different text samples.

title: TransferLearning
text: The premise remains: find a well-performing existing model and apply it to your own problem.

title: TransferLearning
text: Example of transfer learning being applied to computer vision and natural language processing (NLP). In the case of computer vision, a computer vision model might learn patterns on millions of images in ImageNet and then use those patterns to infer on another problem. And for NLP, a language model may learn the structure of language by reading all of Wikipedia (and perhaps more) and then apply that knowledge to a different problem.

title: TransferLearning
text: There are two main benefits to using transfer learning:

title: TransferLearning
text: Can leverage an existing model (usually a neural network architecture) proven to work on problems similar to our own.

title: TransferLearning
text: Can leverage a working model which has already learned patterns on similar data to our own. This often results in achieving great results with less custom data .

title: TransferLearning
text: We'll be putting these to the test for our FoodVision Mini problem, we'll take a computer vision model pretrained on ImageNet and try to leverage its underlying learned representations for classifying images of pizza, steak and sushi.

title: TransferLearning
text: Both research and practice support the use of transfer learning too.

title: TransferLearning
text: A finding from a recent machine learning research paper recommended practitioners use transfer learning wherever possible.

title: TransferLearning
text: A study into the effects of whether training from scratch or using transfer learning was better from a practitioner's point of view, found transfer learning to be far more beneficial in terms of cost and time. Source: How to train your ViT? Data, Augmentation, and Regularization in Vision Transformers paper section 6 (conclusion).

title: TransferLearning
text: And Jeremy Howard (founder of fastai ) is a big proponent of transfer learning.

title: TransferLearning
text: The things that really make a difference (transfer learning), if we can do better at transfer learning, it’s this world changing thing. Suddenly lots more people can do world-class work with less resources and less data. — Jeremy Howard on the Lex Fridman Podcast

title: TransferLearning
text: The world of deep learning is an amazing place.

title: TransferLearning
text: So amazing that many people around the world share their work.

title: TransferLearning
text: Often, code and pretrained models for the latest state-of-the-art research is released within a few days of publishing.

title: TransferLearning
text: And there are several places you can find pretrained models to use for your own problems.

title: TransferLearning
text: With access to such high-quality resources as above, it should be common practice at the start of every deep learning problem you take on to ask, "Does a pretrained model exist for my problem?"

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Note: As of torchvision v0.13+, there's an update to how data transforms can be created using torchvision.models . I've called the previous method "manual creation" and the new method "auto creation". This notebook showcases both.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: When using a pretrained model, it's important that your custom data going into the model is prepared in the same way as the original training data that went into the model .

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Prior to torchvision v0.13+, to create a transform for a pretrained model in torchvision.models , the documentation stated:

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: All pre-trained models expect input images normalized in the same way, i.e. mini-batches of 3-channel RGB images of shape (3 x H x W), where H and W are expected to be at least 224.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: The images have to be loaded in to a range of [0, 1] and then normalized using mean = [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] and std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] .

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: You can use the following transform to normalize:

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text:
normalize = transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                                 std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225])

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: The good news is, we can achieve the above transformations with a combination of:

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Note: some pretrained models from torchvision.models in different sizes to [3, 224, 224] , for example, some might take them in [3, 240, 240] . For specific input image sizes, see the documentation.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Question: Where did the mean and standard deviation values come from? Why do we need to do this?

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: These were calculated from the data. Specifically, the ImageNet dataset by taking the means and standard deviations across a subset of images.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: We also don't need to do this. Neural networks are usually quite capable of figuring out appropriate data distributions (they'll calculate where the mean and standard deviations need to be on their own) but setting them at the start can help our networks achieve better performance quicker.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Let's compose a series of torchvision.transforms to perform the above steps.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: # Create a transforms pipeline manually (required for torchvision < 0.13) manual_transforms = transforms . Compose ([ transforms . Resize (( 224 , 224 )), # 1. Reshape all images to 224x224 (though some models may require different sizes) transforms . ToTensor (), # 2. Turn image values to between 0 & 1 transforms . Normalize ( mean = [ 0.485 , 0.456 , 0.406 ], # 3. A mean of [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] (across each colour channel) std = [ 0.229 , 0.224 , 0.225 ]) # 4. A standard deviation of [0.229, 0.224, 0.225] (across each colour channel), ])

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Wonderful!

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Now we've got a manually created series of transforms ready to prepare our images, let's create training and testing DataLoaders.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: We can create these using the create_dataloaders function from the data_setup.py script we created in 05. PyTorch Going Modular Part 2 .

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: We'll set batch_size=32 so our model sees mini-batches of 32 samples at a time.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: And we can transform our images using the transform pipeline we created above by setting transform=manual_transforms .

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: Note: I've included this manual creation of transforms in this notebook because you may come across resources that use this style. It's also important to note that because these transforms are manually created, they're also infinitely customizable. So if you wanted to include data augmentation techniques in your transforms pipeline, you could.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.1 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (manual creation)
text: # Create training and testing DataLoaders as well as get a list of class names train_dataloader , test_dataloader , class_names = data_setup . create_dataloaders ( train_dir = train_dir , test_dir = test_dir , transform = manual_transforms , # resize, convert images to between 0 & 1 and normalize them batch_size = 32 ) # set mini-batch size to 32 train_dataloader , test_dataloader , class_names

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: As previously stated, when using a pretrained model, it's important that your custom data going into the model is prepared in the same way as the original training data that went into the model .

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: Above we saw how to manually create a transform for a pretrained model.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: But as of torchvision v0.13+, an automatic transform creation feature has been added.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: When you setup a model from torchvision.models and select the pretrained model weights you'd like to use, for example, say we'd like to use:

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: weights = torchvision . models . EfficientNet_B0_Weights . DEFAULT

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: Where,

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: EfficientNet_B0_Weights is the model architecture weights we'd like to use (there are many different model architecture options in torchvision.models ).

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: DEFAULT means the best available weights (the best performance in ImageNet). Note: Depending on the model architecture you choose, you may also see other options such as IMAGENET_V1 and IMAGENET_V2 where generally the higher version number the better. Though if you want the best available, DEFAULT is the easiest option. See the torchvision.models documentation for more.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: Note: Depending on the model architecture you choose, you may also see other options such as IMAGENET_V1 and IMAGENET_V2 where generally the higher version number the better. Though if you want the best available, DEFAULT is the easiest option. See the torchvision.models documentation for more.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: Let's try it out.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: # Get a set of pretrained model weights weights = torchvision . models . EfficientNet_B0_Weights . DEFAULT # .DEFAULT = best available weights from pretraining on ImageNet weights

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: EfficientNet_B0_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: And now to access the transforms associated with our weights , we can use the transforms() method.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: This is essentially saying "get the data transforms that were used to train the EfficientNet_B0_Weights on ImageNet".

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: # Get the transforms used to create our pretrained weights auto_transforms = weights . transforms () auto_transforms

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)

ImageClassification(
    crop_size=[224]
    resize_size=[256]
    mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406]
    std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]
    interpolation=InterpolationMode.BICUBIC
)

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: Notice how auto_transforms is very similar to manual_transforms , the only difference is that auto_transforms came with the model architecture we chose, where as we had to create manual_transforms by hand.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: The benefit of automatically creating a transform through weights.transforms() is that you ensure you're using the same data transformation as the pretrained model used when it was trained.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: However, the tradeoff of using automatically created transforms is a lack of customization.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: We can use auto_transforms to create DataLoaders with create_dataloaders() just as before.

title: TransferLearning
section: 2.2 Creating a transform for torchvision.models (auto creation)
text: # Create training and testing DataLoaders as well as get a list of class names train_dataloader , test_dataloader , class_names = data_setup . create_dataloaders ( train_dir = train_dir , test_dir = test_dir , transform = auto_transforms , # perform same data transforms on our own data as the pretrained model batch_size = 32 ) # set mini-batch size to 32 train_dataloader , test_dataloader , class_names

text: Alright, here comes the fun part!

title: TransferLearning
text: Over the past few notebooks we've been building PyTorch neural networks from scratch.

title: TransferLearning
text: And while that's a good skill to have, our models haven't been performing as well as we'd like.

title: TransferLearning
text: That's where transfer learning comes in.

title: TransferLearning
text: The whole idea of transfer learning is to take an already well-performing model on a problem-space similar to yours and then customise it to your use case .

title: TransferLearning
text: Since we're working on a computer vision problem (image classification with FoodVision Mini), we can find pretrained classification models in torchvision.models .

title: TransferLearning
text: Exploring the documentation, you'll find plenty of common computer vision architecture backbones such as:

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: It depends on your problem/the device you're working with.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: Generally, the higher number in the model name (e.g. efficientnet_b0() -> efficientnet_b1() -> efficientnet_b7() ) means better performance but a larger model.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: You might think better performance is always better , right?

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: That's true but some better performing models are too big for some devices .

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: For example, say you'd like to run your model on a mobile-device, you'll have to take into account the limited compute resources on the device, thus you'd be looking for a smaller model.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: But if you've got unlimited compute power, as The Bitter Lesson states, you'd likely take the biggest, most compute hungry model you can.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: Understanding this performance vs. speed vs. size tradeoff will come with time and practice.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: For me, I've found a nice balance in the efficientnet_bX models.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: As of May 2022, Nutrify (the machine learning powered app I'm working on) is powered by an efficientnet_b0 .

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: Comma.ai (a company that makes open source self-driving car software) uses an efficientnet_b2 to learn a representation of the road.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.1 Which pretrained model should you use?
text: Note: Even though we're using efficientnet_bX , it's important not to get too attached to any one architecture, as they are always changing as new research gets released. Best to experiment, experiment, experiment and see what works for your problem.

title: TransferLearning
text: The pretrained model we're going to be using is torchvision.models.efficientnet_b0() .

title: TransferLearning
text: The architecture is from the paper EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks .

title: TransferLearning
text: Example of what we're going to create, a pretrained EfficientNet_B0 model from torchvision.models with the output layer adjusted for our use case of classifying pizza, steak and sushi images.

title: TransferLearning
text: We can setup the EfficientNet_B0 pretrained ImageNet weights using the same code as we used to create the transforms.

title: TransferLearning
text: weights = torchvision . models . EfficientNet_B0_Weights . DEFAULT # .DEFAULT = best available weights for ImageNet

title: TransferLearning
text: This means the model has already been trained on millions of images and has a good base representation of image data.

title: TransferLearning
text: The PyTorch version of this pretrained model is capable of achieving ~77.7% accuracy across ImageNet's 1000 classes.

title: TransferLearning
text: We'll also send it to the target device.

title: TransferLearning
text: # OLD: Setup the model with pretrained weights and send it to the target device (this was prior to torchvision v0.13) # model = torchvision.models.efficientnet_b0(pretrained=True).to(device) # OLD method (with pretrained=True) # NEW: Setup the model with pretrained weights and send it to the target device (torchvision v0.13+) weights = torchvision . models . EfficientNet_B0_Weights . DEFAULT # .DEFAULT = best available weights model = torchvision . models . efficientnet_b0 ( weights = weights ) . to ( device ) #model # uncomment to output (it's very long)

title: TransferLearning
text: Note: In previous versions of torchvision , you'd create a pretrained model with code like:

title: TransferLearning
text: model = torchvision.models.efficientnet_b0(pretrained=True).to(device)

title: TransferLearning
text: However, running this using torchvision v0.13+ will result in errors such as the following:

title: TransferLearning
text: UserWarning: The parameter 'pretrained' is deprecated since 0.13 and will be removed in 0.15, please use 'weights' instead.

title: TransferLearning
text: And...

title: TransferLearning
text: UserWarning: Arguments other than a weight enum or None for weights are deprecated since 0.13 and will be removed in 0.15. The current behavior is equivalent to passing weights=EfficientNet_B0_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1. You can also use weights=EfficientNet_B0_Weights.DEFAULT to get the most up-to-date weights.

title: TransferLearning
text: If we print the model, we get something similar to the following:

title: TransferLearning
text: Lots and lots and lots of layers.

title: TransferLearning
text: This is one of the benefits of transfer learning, taking an existing model, that's been crafted by some of the best engineers in the world and applying to your own problem.

title: TransferLearning
text: Our efficientnet_b0 comes in three main parts:

title: TransferLearning
text: features - A collection of convolutional layers and other various activation layers to learn a base representation of vision data (this base representation/collection of layers is often referred to as features or feature extractor , "the base layers of the model learn the different features of images").

title: TransferLearning
text: avgpool - Takes the average of the output of the features layer(s) and turns it into a feature vector .

title: TransferLearning
text: classifier - Turns the feature vector into a vector with the same dimensionality as the number of required output classes (since efficientnet_b0 is pretrained on ImageNet and because ImageNet has 1000 classes, out_features=1000 is the default).
