section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: The process of transfer learning usually goes: freeze some base layers of a pretrained model (typically the features section) and then adjust the output layers (also called head/classifier layers) to suit your needs.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: You can customise the outputs of a pretrained model by changing the output layer(s) to suit your problem. The original torchvision.models.efficientnet_b0() comes with out_features=1000 because there are 1000 classes in ImageNet, the dataset it was trained on. However, for our problem, classifying images of pizza, steak and sushi we only need out_features=3 .

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Let's freeze all of the layers/parameters in the features section of our efficientnet_b0 model.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Note: To freeze layers means to keep them how they are during training. For example, if your model has pretrained layers, to freeze them would be to say, "don't change any of the patterns in these layers during training, keep them how they are." In essence, we'd like to keep the pretrained weights/patterns our model has learned from ImageNet as a backbone and then only change the output layers.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: We can freeze all of the layers/parameters in the features section by setting the attribute requires_grad=False .

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: For parameters with requires_grad=False , PyTorch doesn't track gradient updates and in turn, these parameters won't be changed by our optimizer during training.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: In essence, a parameter with requires_grad=False is "untrainable" or "frozen" in place.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: # Freeze all base layers in the "features" section of the model (the feature extractor) by setting requires_grad=False for param in model . features . parameters (): param . requires_grad = False

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Feature extractor layers frozen!

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Let's now adjust the output layer or the classifier portion of our pretrained model to our needs.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Right now our pretrained model has out_features=1000 because there are 1000 classes in ImageNet.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: However, we don't have 1000 classes, we only have three, pizza, steak and sushi.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: We can change the classifier portion of our model by creating a new series of layers.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: The current classifier consists of:

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text:
(classifier): Sequential(
    (0): Dropout(p=0.2, inplace=True)
    (1): Linear(in_features=1280, out_features=1000, bias=True)

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: We'll keep the Dropout layer the same using torch.nn.Dropout(p=0.2, inplace=True) .

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Note: Dropout layers randomly remove connections between two neural network layers with a probability of p . For example, if p=0.2 , 20% of connections between neural network layers will be removed at random each pass. This practice is meant to help regularize (prevent overfitting) a model by making sure the connections that remain learn features to compensate for the removal of the other connections (hopefully these remaining features are more general ).

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: And we'll keep in_features=1280 for our Linear output layer but we'll change the out_features value to the length of our class_names ( len(['pizza', 'steak', 'sushi']) = 3 ).

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Our new classifier layer should be on the same device as our model .

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: # Set the manual seeds torch . manual_seed ( 42 ) torch . cuda . manual_seed ( 42 ) # Get the length of class_names (one output unit for each class) output_shape = len ( class_names ) # Recreate the classifier layer and seed it to the target device model . classifier = torch . nn . Sequential ( torch . nn . Dropout ( p = 0.2 , inplace = True ), torch . nn . Linear ( in_features = 1280 , out_features = output_shape , # same number of output units as our number of classes bias = True )) . to ( device )

text: Ho, ho! There's a fair few changes here!

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Let's go through them:

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Trainable column - You'll see that many of the base layers (the ones in the features portion) have their Trainable value as False . This is because we set their attribute requires_grad=False . Unless we change this, these layers won't be updated during future training.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Output shape of classifier - The classifier portion of the model now has an Output Shape value of [32, 3] instead of [32, 1000] . It's Trainable value is also True . This means its parameters will be updated during training. In essence, we're using the features portion to feed our classifier portion a base representation of an image and then our classifier layer is going to learn how to base representation aligns with our problem.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Less trainable parameters - Previously there were 5,288,548 trainable parameters. But since we froze many of the layers of the model and only left the classifier as trainable, there's now only 3,843 trainable parameters (even less than our TinyVGG model). Though there's also 4,007,548 non-trainable parameters, these will create a base representation of our input images to feed into our classifier layer.

title: TransferLearning
section: 3.4 Freezing the base model and changing the output layer to suit our needs
text: Note: The more trainable parameters a model has, the more compute power/longer it takes to train. Freezing the base layers of our model and leaving it with less trainable parameters means our model should train quite quickly. This is one huge benefit of transfer learning, taking the already learned parameters of a model trained on a problem similar to yours and only tweaking the outputs slightly to suit your problem.

title: TransferLearning
text: Now we've got a pretrained model that's semi-frozen and has a customised classifier , how about we see transfer learning in action?

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: One thing we'll have to remember is that for our model to make predictions on an image, the image has to be in same format as the images our model was trained on.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: This means we'll need to make sure our images have:

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Same shape - If our images are different shapes to what our model was trained on, we'll get shape errors.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Same datatype - If our images are a different datatype (e.g. torch.int8 vs. torch.float32 ) we'll get datatype errors.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Same device - If our images are on a different device to our model, we'll get device errors.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Same transformations - If our model is trained on images that have been transformed in certain way (e.g. normalized with a specific mean and standard deviation) and we try and make predictions on images transformed in a different way, these predictions may be off.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Note: These requirements go for all kinds of data if you're trying to make predictions with a trained model. Data you'd like to predict on should be in the same format as your model was trained on.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: To do all of this, we'll create a function pred_and_plot_image() to:

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Take in a trained model, a list of class names, a filepath to a target image, an image size, a transform and a target device.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Open an image with PIL.Image.open() .

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Create a transform for the image (this will default to the manual_transforms we created above or it could use a transform generated from weights.transforms() ).

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Make sure the model is on the target device.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Turn on model eval mode with model.eval() (this turns off layers like nn.Dropout() , so they aren't used for inference) and the inference mode context manager.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Transform the target image with the transform made in step 3 and add an extra batch dimension with torch.unsqueeze(dim=0) so our input image has shape [batch_size, color_channels, height, width] .

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Make a prediction on the image by passing it to the model ensuring it's on the target device.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Convert the model's output logits to prediction probabilities with torch.softmax() .

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Convert model's prediction probabilities to prediction labels with torch.argmax() .

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Plot the image with matplotlib and set the title to the prediction label from step 9 and prediction probability from step 8.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: Note: This is a similar function to 04. PyTorch Custom Datasets section 11.3's pred_and_plot_image() with a few tweaked steps.

title: TransferLearning
section: 6. Make predictions on images from the test set
text: from typing import List , Tuple from PIL import Image # 1. Take in a trained model, class names, image path, image size, a transform and target device def pred_and_plot_image ( model : torch . nn . Module , image_path : str , class_names : List [ str ], image_size : Tuple [ int , int ] = ( 224 , 224 ), transform : torchvision . transforms = None , device : torch . device = device ): # 2. Open image img = Image . open ( image_path ) # 3. Create transformation for image (if one doesn't exist) if transform is not None : image_transform = transform else : image_transform = transforms . Compose ([ transforms . Resize ( image_size ), transforms . ToTensor (), transforms . Normalize ( mean = [ 0.485 , 0.456 , 0.406 ], std = [ 0.229 , 0.224 , 0.225 ]), ]) ### Predict on image ### # 4. Make sure the model is on the target device model . to ( device ) # 5. Turn on model evaluation mode and inference mode model . eval () with torch . inference_mode (): # 6. Transform and add an extra dimension to image (model requires samples in [batch_size, color_channels, height, width]) transformed_image = image_transform ( img ) . unsqueeze ( dim = 0 ) # 7. Make a prediction on image with an extra dimension and send it to the target device target_image_pred = model ( transformed_image . to ( device )) # 8. Convert logits -> prediction probabilities (using torch.softmax() for multi-class classification) target_image_pred_probs = torch . softmax ( target_image_pred , dim = 1 ) # 9. Convert prediction probabilities -> prediction labels target_image_pred_label = torch . argmax ( target_image_pred_probs , dim = 1 ) # 10. Plot image with predicted label and probability plt . figure () plt . imshow ( img ) plt . title ( f "Pred: { class_names [ target_image_pred_label ] } | Prob: { target_image_pred_probs . max () : .3f } " ) plt . axis ( False );
